subtopic: PROPOSAL TO PENALIZE PRACTICE OF ISSUING CHEQUES WITHOUT FUNDS

speechtext:
Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 43 to amend the criminal code.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this
bill is to make it easier, or perhaps I should say to make it less impossible, to secure a conviction against that ever growing band of crooks who make it their business to prey on the public b}' going from town to town and from district to district leaving behind them a trail of cheques drawn on banks where they have no funds or where in many cases they even never had an account. At the present time these men can be proceeded against only under the section of the criminal code which deals with false pretences and it has been found almost impossible to secure a conviction under that section. It is necessary to show an evil intent when the cheque was passed, that is, an intent to defraud the payee, and it is practically impossible to prove what is in a man's mind on a given occasion. Very often the plea is made: Yes, I knew I had no money in the bank but I expected President Hoover or someone else to make a deposit before it came due. It is very necessary to check this growing evil which imposes a heavy burden on hotels and business men, which burden is ultimately passed on to the consuming public. This will be rather a difficult piece of legislation because it is essential while proceeding against this type of man to protect two classes of individuals. The first is the man who by mere inadvertence allows his account to become overdrawn. I have done that myself, and that man must be protected. Then there is the other man, almost equally innocent, who is running a small business. Times are hard and he is being pressed, we will say, by his wholesaler. He knows it will take four or five days for a cheque to reach the wholesaler and then be returned to his bank; he knows he is getting money in all the time from his customers and he takes a chance and draws a cheque which may not be good at the moment but which he honestly expects will, in all probability, be good by the time it comes back to his
Privilege-Mr. Cayley

bank. That man should be protected, and this bill fully protects these two classes of individual.
If the house will allow me to introduce this bill and have it read the first time, I will not press the second reading so that perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) may consider it, and boards of trade, chambers of commerce and business men throughout the country will be given an opportunity to express their views.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF EXCHANGE PRIVILEGES OFFERED TO HOLDERS OF GOVERNMENT BONDS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER OF EXCHANGE PRIVILEGES OFFERED TO HOLDERS OF GOVERNMENT BONDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promised the house yesterday that I would make a general statement with respect to the proposed conversion loan. During the years of the war the Canadian people loaned the government of Canada 853,000.000, payable in October, 1931, with interest at 5 per cent per annum; 873,000,000, payable November 1, 1932, with interest at per cent per annum; 8446,000,000, payable on November 1, 1933, with interest at 5^ per cent per annum, and 8511,000,000, payable on November 1, 1934, with interest at 5^ per cent per annum. The total amount of these four loans is $1,083,000,000, and it will be ob-

served that nearly one billion dollars of this amount falls due in November, 1933, and November, 1934. These loans will either have to be paid or renewed and it is obviously impossible that they can be paid except by the flotation of new securities, the proceeds to be used to liquidate the old loans.
At the moment this large obligation is a serious menace to our financial operations because it is felt that as long as these liabilities have to be met in successive years there will be increasing difficulties in connection with the handling of such transactions. The government, with the best advice available, has concluded that it is desirable to anticipate the maturity of these obligations and has created what will be known as the Dominion of Canada conversion loan, 1931. No new money will be sought but the old securities will be exchanged for new bonds bearing a rate of interest of 4} per cent per annum. All interest provided by the former securities and any benefits and privileges created thereby will remain intact until maturity.
On Monday next every newspaper in Canada will contain a full statement on the proposed conversion loan and I do not think it is necessary to do more at the moment than to merely indicate the general reasons which have actuated the government in taking this action.
Before taking any final steps in this matter, the government was fortunate in being able to set up with the aid of the banks and bond houses of Canada a central committee, the chairman of which is Sir Charles Gordon, president of the Bank of Montreal and the vicechairman, Mr. Victor Drury of Montreal. The 'Canadian Bank of Commerce is represented by Mr. S. H. Logan, its general manager; the Bank of Nova Scotia by Mr. J. A. McLeod, its general manager; the Banque Camadienne Nationale by Mr. Beaudry Leman, its general manager and the Royal Bank of Canada by Mr. M. W. Wilson, its general manager. The bond houses in Toronto are represented by Mr. Arthur F. White, of the Dominion Securities Corporation, Mr. H. R. Tudhope of A. E. Ames & Company, and Mr. J. H. Gundy, of Wood Gundy & Company. The bond houses in Montreal are represented by Mr. Drury and Mr. E. G. Hanson of Hanson Brothers. In addition to that, Mr. G. W. Spinney, one of the executive officers of the Bank of Montreal, has given unremitting toil to this transaction and, while not a member of the committee, has undertaken large responsibilities in connection therewith.
The plan involves the participation by and cooperation of 4,500 agencies throughout Canada, including the branches of all the char-

Conversion Loan-Mr. Bennett
tered banks of Canada and of the recognized bond dealers and brokers. I need hardly say that in a country as large as Canada it is important that the same opportunity be afforded on the same day to every person interested and it therefore becomes necessary to prepare very large quantities of material to be made available on Monday next in every part of Canada. It will perhaps sup-prise the house to know that during the iast seven days orders for over 8,000,000 forms have been placed with the, Printing Bureau and that the major portion of this large order has been delivered to the Department of Finance. Prior to noon to-day, actually
4,850,000	forms had been shipped by the Department of Finance to various depositories established throughout Canada. Five hundred thousand interim certificates in various denominations from 8100 to $100,000 are being printed and distributed to the offices of the receiver general throughout Canada. We expect that on Monday next the interim certificates for those who wish to exchange the old bonds for the new, will be available for the full amount of the loan, and therefore the conversion may be made promptly.
The Post Office Department has done a great deal of work in expediting the transmission of mail, because in large cities like Montreal and Toronto, this has imposed upon that department a great additional effort. The campaign is for the moment limited to the conversion of $250,000,000 of the old securities. The books will open on Monday next and it is proposed that the, Minister of Finance shall have a discretion as to the closing of them, otherwise they will close on the 23rd of May. Whatever additional information any hon. member may desire to receive will, of course, be available on Monday morning through the press, but I do not think any useful purpose will be served by stating more than I have indicated as to the purpose and intention of the government in making this conversion at this time.
It is the belief of the government and those best qualified to speak with authority in Canada, that a conversion or exchange of this kind at this time will be of a two-fold advantage to this country. In the first place it will do something to remove from the horizon a dark cloud of impending borrowing that every Minister of Finance must face as long as there is $1,000,000,000 to be liquidated in some way between now and 1934. In the second place, inasmuch as the securities are largely held by Canadians, it is believed that by accepting, after the date of maturity of the present obligations, a rate of interest one per cent less than that which they have been receiving, they will indicate a faith and belief
in the future of their country that will be a striking testimony to the value of its assets and its credit amongst the peoples of the world. I do not think it is necessary to take up further time than to indicate in this general way what the purpose of the government has been in this regard.

speechtext:
I promised yesterday to make a statement with regard to the operations of the Canadian farm loan board. This morning I had prepared a short memorandum, part of which I shall now submit to the house:
The Canadian farm loan board is constituted and operates as a body corporate and politic under the provisions of a special act of parliament which defines its powers and duties, namely, chapter 66, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927.
The members of the board are appointed for a term of years by order in council of the Dominion government. The administration of the board's activities, however, in each province iR carried out through the agency of a provincial board of three members all of whom are the nominees of the provincial government. Provision is made also for the appointment of a fourth member to each provincial board who shall be the nominee of the borrowers in that province.
The Dominion government provided the initial financial assistance for the board in the form of advances of capital up to five million dollars which are free of interest for three years from date of advance.

Farm Loan Board-Mr. Bennett
That is to say, the government of Canada advances the money to the board which for the first three years is free from any interest charge in favour of the country; the country for the first three years gets nothing for its money. The memorandum continues:
The amount of the said advances, however, with interest, after the initial three-year period, at the rate of five per cent per annum, is repayable out of the earnings of the board. Subsequent loaning funds are obtained through the sale by the board of farm loan bonds issued on the security of mortgages held by the board on account of loans already made. These bonds do not carry the guarantee of the government and the payment of interest on the said bonds and the repayment of capital must 'be provided for by the board itself.
As a body corporate, the board under the act is empowered to issue capital stock. The subscribers to the said stock are limited to three classes:-[DOT]
The Dominion government purchases stock of the board to the extent of five per cent of moneys loaned by the board;
Each provincial government subscribes to stock of the board to the extent of five per cent of moneys loaned in the province;
Each borrower subscribes to stock of the board to the extent of five per cent of the loan obtained.
All earnings derived by the board in the course of its operations, after providing the necessary reserves, are distributed to the shareholders in the form of dividends. Dividends on stock held by the governments, however, are limited to five per cent per annum, the borrower shareholders alone participating in dividends declared in excess of this amount.
In the interests of all shareholders, the Dominion government appoints a firm of chartered accountants to make an annual audit of the board's affairs and this report-
As perhaps the house will recollect:
[DOT]-is tabled in parliament.
As protection to the interests of the provincial governments, provision is made under the act for the convening by the Minister of Finance from time to time of an advisory council consisting of the provincial treasurers and the chief executive officer of each provincial board to confer on matters relating to the administration of the board.
As an assurance to shareholders that the board shall riot in its regulations exceed the powers given to it under the provisions of the act, the regulations of the board are subject to approval by the governor in council.
As is apparent from the foregoing, the whole scheme of administration and the financial structure of the board is entirely different from the structure of the provincial boards which are or have been operating in the various provinces of Canada.
In the case of the various provincial boards, loaning funds of the board have been provided either directly by vote of the provincial legislature or through the sale of government guaranteed securities and all the earnings of these boards in turn have been directly accounted for by the provincial board as received to the provincial government.
Assuming the loans had been made, and many have been, the next question is as to
the policy of the board with respect to the collection of the interest and the principal. That question being asked yesterday, I asked the chairman of the board, Dr. J. D. MacLean, as to what .that policy was, and he has submitted the following memorandum:
The policy of the board with respect to arrears, which recently went forward to the various provincial offices, is outlined in the form of a memorandum, as follows:
"The general policy of the board in dealing with cases of arrears must be framed along the following lines:
(a)	In cases where there is actual inability of the borrower to pay, carry the borrower over for a reasonable length of time, provided,

1.	He is making an honest effort to pay and is giving the board equal consideration with other creditors.
2.	There are reasonable prospects of ability to pay within a reasonable length of time.
3.	The security is not deteriorating in value, and the amount of the board's loan plus arrears and unpaid taxes has not grown to an amount which jeopardizes the board's prospects of realizing by sales proceedings the amount of the board's investment.
Naturally, where the borrower's intentions are the best but where there is no reasonable prospect of the applicant improving his position either because of other liabilities or because of lack of farming ability, and where the postponement of action means no ultimate relief to the borrower there is no object in withholding the institution of sale proceedings.
(b)	Where there is ability to pay but failure to do so, the failure of the applicant to furnish either satisfactory collateral security to secure payment within a reasonable length of time or to give other satisfactory assurance of payment should be followed by either a distress on chattels or the commencement of foreclosure proceedings whichever is, under the circumstances. most appropriate.
In view of the importance attached by head office to the necessity of following up collections in the early stages of the board's loaning operations we request that starting May 1st every superintendent forward a brief monthly report on each case of arrears."
That is the memorandum sent to the provincial offices. Dr. MacLean continues:
The provincial boards have placed on each borrower who has professed inability to pay the onus of giving to the board satisfactory reasons for an extension of time for payment. Each such borrower has been required to submit a statement of crop returns and a statement of receipts and expenditures covering the last year's operations and an up-to-date statement of assets and liabilities, with a view to determining whether or not a good case has been made out for an extension of time for payment.
All borrowers who have given what appeared to be reliable undertakings for future payment, or who, as the result of the year's operations, are actually financially unable to make a payment until proceeds of present year's crops are received, are granted the necessary extension of time. In cases, howeverwhere the borrower has not displayed any inclination to cooperate with the board nor to give satisfactory information or replies to letters from the board, solicitor's collection letters have gone forward. In other cases, where there appears to be
1386	COMMONS
Farm Loan Board-Mr. Bennett
ability to pay but the failure to do bo, distress warrants have been issued, to enforce collections.
I may say that in the province of Alberta, where we have the largest percentage of arrears at the present time, no foreclosure or sale proceedings have been instituted in any case up to the present time. Distress warrants have been issued in not more than ten cases, and in each case where such distress warrant has been issued the borrower has made a satisfactory payment very shortly after seizure was effected.
Solicitors' letters have gone forward in all provinces, however, to a percentage of borrowers who had failed either to carry out the promises previously made, or who had failed to make a satisfactory response to communications from the board.
The responsibility of collection rests with the provincial board of each province. Distress proceedings may be instituted by the provincial superintendent on the authority of the provincial board. Sale or foreclosure proceedings, however, are instituted only on instructions from head office upon the recommendation of the provincial board.	_
Reinspection reports on the securities held bv the board in as many cases of arrears as possible will be obtained during the course of the present season.
I trust that two points are abundantly clear, two points about which there has, apparently, been some doubt:	First, that
the government of Canada is not responsible for the initiation of proceedings in connection with collections; secondly, that there can be no foreclosure proceedings taken or sale under foreclosure proceedings made unless the head office does give its authority. I think it is also patent to everyone that the board itself is an organization over which the government as such has no control; in other words, it is not an instrument of government; it is an organization created by a statute, and is discharging its statutory obligations with the assistance given by the governments of the country, federal and provincial, and by borrowers from the funds which it may have at its disposal.
In the Finance department this morning I received from Mr. Sellar the last report of the federal farm loan board of the United States for the year ending December 31, 1930, and I venture to read two or three lines from the opening pages of that report because I conceive them to be of some importance in this country where our experience has been limited as compared with the very large experience which the farm loan board of the United States has had in the conduct of business of this character.
The chairman indicates the effort made to -shall I say?-place the business of the board in politics by introducing measures in the House of Representatives that on the one hand would force action on the part of the board or on the other restrict its activities.

At page 5 of the report I find the following:
In this connection a number of bills and resolutions have been introduced in both houses of congress providing for the suspension of foreclosures by the federal land banks in certain sections of the country for varying periods of time or the extension of the time of payment of instalments on loans due the Danks and authorizing loans by the government to the federal land banks to enable them to defer foreclosures. These measures in effect would result in the establishment of a moratorium on payments. The secretary of the treasury, in response to requests from the committees on banking and currency of the Senate and house for his recommendations, has reported adversely with respect to these proposals. In the opinion of the board measures of this character would impair the morale of borrowers generally,' encourage delinquencies on a widespread scale, imperil the market for federal land bank bonds and do incalculable harm to the system. Incidentally it should not be overlooked that, as only about 12 per cent of the farm mortgage indebtedness of the country is held by the federal land banks, such measures, even if enacted into law, would not affect a large number of the farmers in the sections concerned.
The board is advised that many borrowers in a position to pay have not paid promptly because they understood that they would be granted extensions by law and that the banks would be prohibited from taking action for self protection. This presented an unfortunate condition, and it was a serious problem for the banks to correct these impressions and misunderstandings. For example, one borrower from a federal land bank pinned a newspaper clipping, announcing the introduction of a bill proposing an extension of the time of payment, to the notice which the bank had sent him regarding the instalment on his loan -which was due and returned it to the bank without payment. In another case one of the banks received from a delinquent borrower a copy of a letter which had been written to him, pointing out that legislation had been proposed extending the time for making payments on loans and stating that some form of relief as to extensions likely would be made. A field man of one of tbe banks reported that he found "numerous cases of the least deserving just suspending their efforts to make the payment and feeling confident that they will be relieved." These instances are cited merely as illustrations of the effect that even the introduction and consideration of the proposals had in increasing the collection problems of the banks, which, of course, as stated above, must make all the collections possible in any event.
There is also in the report an extract from the recommendations of the secretary of the treasury, but I will not trespass upon the time of this house to read them. It will be observed the problem to which attention has been directed is not one peculiar to Canada, but one which has to be dealt with in every country where this form of organization exists. Fortunately or unfortunately in this case, so far as the government is concerned, we have no power to deal with the matter in the sense in which the question was asked yesterday.

Business of the House
Power must be exercised through the provincial boards, and I have every reason to believe that every possible consideration has been extended to borrowers who are also shareholders in the board for the purpose of enabling those who have hope and confidence in the future to carry on and succeed in deriving from their efforts such sums as will enable them to liquidate their obligations.

subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDEE 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called I think it is desirable that there should be an understanding between the government and other hon. members of the house as to the business of the day. Last night at the conclusion of the sitting the question was raised as to the significance of standing order 28. That standing order is as follows:
28. On Thursday and Fridays when the order of the day is called for the house to go into committee of supply, or of ways and means, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question, providing that, except by the unanimous consent of the house, the estimates of each department shall be first taken up on a day other than Thursday or Friday.
I assume therefore if order No. 5 is called, "House again in committee of supply," Your Honour will leave the chair without question being put. For that reason, as the matter is one which affects the privileges of the house, I wish to raise the point I do before Your Honour leaves the chair. Under standing order No. 28 I assume that with the exception of estimates which have been taken up on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday, the government will not have the right to proceed, except by consent of the house, with estimates of any department other than those which have been discussed on those days. The only estimates which have been discussed on Mondays, Tuesdays or Wednesdays have been the estimates of the Department of Public Works, and the government would be perfectly in order to-daj to proceed with the estimates of that department. If, however, the government were to proceed with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs they would have to have the consent of the house so to proceed. Last night I intimated that in order to meet a certain purpose to which the Prime Minister referred, so far as the official opposition was concerned we would consent to proceeding with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, by the
calling of a certain item to-day. I was surprised when I found that the Prime Minister felt he had a right to proceed to-day with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. He apparently assumed such to be the case simply because yesterday we consented to allow him, for yesterday only, to take up an item in that particular department. Not only did we consent to take up the item but we consented to the passing of it. I am not raising this question for any factious reason or to embarrass the government. speechtext:
Except by consent. I
sat in the position which my right hon. friend now occupies during a period of some three years and learned something in connection with the transaction of parliamentary business, and I recall very distinctly that a similar situation then arose. The difficulty at that time was to determine whether or not the result of the adjournment of a debate, either by reason of the eleven o'clock rule on an ordinary day or the six o'clock rule on Wednesday, was to carry the debate arising out of an amendment on going into supply to the next Thursday, skipping the Wednesday intervening, or to the next Tuesday. Last year we departed from a practice that had theretofore existed, and it was determined then that we should go forward into the next Tuesday unless by consent it was determined otherwise. So, first, there is no difference between the right hon. gentleman and myseif with respect to the necessity of preserving the rule; secondly, the rule can only be abrogated by unanimous consent in the terms of the rule itself; thirdly, that consent was given yesterday. As a result of that consent the committee of supply is seized of the items relating to the Department of Trade and Commerce, and once it is seized of them, and the Speaker is out of the chair, supply then with respect to these items is before the oommittee. In other words, you cannot be out and in at the same time. That is all. The only difference-about which I think the right hon. gentleman has used somewhat stronger language than the facts would warrant-is with regard to what was covered oy the consent. Not once, but three times, and almost a fourth time, I said except by consent we could not go on. With that consent we went into committee of supply, and my hon. friend from Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) followed my right hon. friend a moment later and said he thought we should deal with only one department. I said at once that we desired to deal with more than one branch at least, and that was because of my desire to accommodate the hon. member for Vegreville, for reasons which I made apparent.
Now once more if the house will be good enough to look at the rule it will be found that the difficulty suggested is more imaginary than real. This is the rule that:
On Thursdays and Fridays when the order of the day is called for the house to go into committee of supply, or of ways and means, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question,-
That is tcwday, Friday, he leaves the chair without question put.
-provided that, except by the unanimous consent of the house, the estimates of each department shall be first taken up on a day other than Thursday or Friday.
Yesterday, exactly within the terms of that rule, by the unanimous consent of the house, the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the Department of External Affairs were taken up and an item passed in each, so that we come distinctly and positively within those very words "unanimous consent of the house." All that my submission was or ever has been is that that having been done, and to-day being Friday, on the Speaker leaving the chair, we have before us three departments, and three only, Public Works, Trade and Commerce, and External Affairs; and that it is competent to call items in any one of those departments because they are there, two of them by unanimous consent of this house, and that once being there they cannot be taken out except in the manner and form provided by the rules themselves, namely, after consideration when the committee of supply is determined and its report made. That is the position, otherwise no purpose would be served at all.
But I think the difficulty can be resolved very simply. Last evening we entered into a discussion before the Speaker. He had no jurisdiction because the matter cannot arise before him; it must arise in committee after

Business of the House

the Speaker leaves the chair. Of course, it may ultimately be dealt with by him. I did not then treat the matter as other than a suggestion by the right hon. gentleman opposite as being one that involved the exercise by the Speaker of his official functions, because he could not at that time deal with it. I say to the right hon. gentleman that I am greatly obliged for the suggestion he made in the latter part of his speech. I would not have thought of taking up the time of the house in dealing with the matter had he not made his statement in the terms he did.
I assure him he will never have any cause to complain that the utmost good faith has not been observed by me or by anyone associated with me on this side in the transaction of business, and I am sorry he saw fit, in the light of the consent so graciously given yesterday on three occasions, which enable us to expedite the country's business, to have spoken as he has done. I did find it a little difficult to understand just why he should have taken the view he did. I find it more difficult now to imagine why he should animadvert on our motives in dealing with the matter in the way we did; but if we take up the item to which reference was made yesterday, that with respect to Geneva, and then proceed with public works, we will probably get through with that department. I think that some confusion has arisen with respect to two things. Perhaps I was responsible for part of it in this sense, that I said the effect of the action was to make Thursday Tuesday. Once the debate was ended I realized I could not go into supply on Trade and Commerce, and I went over and consulted with my right hon. friend, with the result that the matter was dealt with as indicated. On three separate occasions, and partially on a fourth, I said I could proceed only by unanimous consent, and it was on that basis, the unanimous consent of this house, that every step has been taken in dealing with this department. I am sure that on further consideration the right hon. gentleman will realize that not only was there neither intention, nor desire nor effort to take advantage of the consent thus given, but that,

on the contrary, an endeavour was made to avail ourselves of that consent for the purpose of carrying forward *what I believe was contemplated, namely, the transaction of the business of the country as expeditiously as possible.

The above petition deals with the alleged infractions of the treaty signed on June 28, 1919, between Poland and the associated and allied powers. It also calls for a committee to consider an impartial inquiry into the facts. From information that I have gathered from the Ukrainian Veterans' Association, the Ukrainian Self Reliance League, the personal experiences of Miss Sheepshanks and Doctor Dey, the accounts of foreign correspondents in Poland, as well as from other reliable sources, I have no doubt that there are very serious infractions of the provisions of that treaty. As proof thereof witness the diabolical methods of racial extermination revealed by Miss Sheepshanks. The manner in which the punitive expeditions referred to in her report were earned out against the Ukrainian minority in Poland, the fiendish application of collective responsibility for individual acts of unsubstantiated sabotage, the wholesale punishment of innocent men, women and children-all constitute an absolute infringement of the following provision of article 2 of the above treaty:
Poland undertakes to assure full and complete protection of life and liberty to all inhabitants of Poland without distinction of birth, nationality, language or religion.
Miss Sheepshanks says that the repressive measures were ordered not because of individual acts of incendiarism but in order to terrorize the population into voting for the government list in the elections. Imagine what would happen in Canada if any party tried to gain power that way. Otherwise why should these expeditions have been sent into villages where no acts of sabotage or incendiarism had ever occurred? Why were 20 Ukrainian members of the Polish Senate arrested and subjected to frightful treatment in a Polish prison? Why was election literature in favour of Ukrainian candidates prohibited, ballot boxes plugged, voters terrorized and struck from lists, and election candidates imprisoned without charge or trial, if it was not to facilitate the election of Pilsudski and his bloodthirsty henchmen? Is it not, sir, a plain violation of article 7 of the above treaty which provides that:
All Polish nationals shall be equal before the law and shall enjoy the same civil and political rights without distinction as to race, language or religion.
The methodical terrorization of the Ukrainians included the indiscriminate extermination of athletic and reading clubs, cultural and economic associations, and schools, both public and private.
Notwithstanding the stipulation under article 9, ensuring the use of the Ukrainian

language as a medium of instruction in the primary schools, I might add that out of over
3,000	Ukrainian schools that existed when Poland took over Eastern Galicia, only about 400 survived her tender care; and out of 17 Ukrainian high schools, the few that are left are being gradually forced to succumb to the influence of a harsh and methodical Polon-ization.
The Ukrainian colleges-
Says a correspondent.
[DOT]-affiliated with the Lemberg university were closed and the Ukrainians applying for admittance were put on quota and were asked to sign very humiliating declarations.
These shameful conditions caused the scattering of the Ukrainian students seeking higher education all over Europe, while many of them, not being able to finance themselves in other countries of Europe, were forced to form a secret Ukrainian university, which was incessantly persecuted by the Polish police. It was quite a usual occurrence for whole classes of students to be arrested en masse and paraded through the city to jails to the accompaniment of the jeers of the Polish populace.
On taking over the Ukrainian territories, the Polish government signed a special pledge to create a separate Ukrainian university by the end of October, 1924. So far the government has not even voted enough money to buy a load of bricks for that university. Just imagine! Seven million Ukrainians carrying one-third of the burdens of the state,-without a university."
Churches, libraries, reading rooms, and economic institutions present the same deplorable picture. If hon. members could for a moment visualize the Royal Canadian Mounted Police demolishing our places of worship, the public libraries, the homes of our families, the central wheat pool office in Winnipeg and all other cooperative buildings in the west, they would get some idea of the terrible and wanton destruction of property that is being carried on in eastern Galicia. What makes the situation more tragic is the fact that the very proprietors of these dearly acquired possessions were forced by the Polish Uhlans to pull down their own buildings and perform all this destruction on their own property. A dispassionate observer of these uncalled for depredations is reported to have said:
If the Poles were as capable of building as they are of destroying there would be no need for such excesses in Poland.

May I quote the
Polish Ameryka Echo, published at Toledo, Ohio. In its issue of November 30, 1930, it has the following:
All those punitive military expeditions into peaceful Ukrainian villages, in particular, into villages where no acts of sabotage were committed, have, by their savage conduct, beatings and tortures of innocent people, achieved this -that Poland has alienated the whole civilized world, while the Ukrainians have been made her irreconcilable enemies.
With respect to this charge of incendiarism, allow me to read an article that appeared in the Daily Illustrated Courier of October 4, 1930. I may say that this is one of the most widely circulated and the most extreme chauvinistic newspaper in Poland. It says:
For some months we have been calling the attention of the public to the fact that the recently observed insurance policy, based upon the increased valuation of movable goods and carried on for the purpose of securing higher premiums, gives a direct incentive to incendiarism. The facts of daily experiences now confirm our prediction of consequences, which can to-day be observed in every part of
Poland	 Conflagrations have recently
assumed great dimensions. In a whole series of municipalities the farms of large estates or the corn-stacks standing on such estates have been victimized. It is significant to note that in the majority of cases the persons found guilty of originating the fires have been none other than the owners of the damaged objects. The fires were crimes of arson perpetrated for gain.
This quotation, as I say, comes from the most chauvinistic newspaper published in Poland. It will be observed that it says that these burnings were not limited to any particular district where the Ukrainians were predominant, but happened throughout the length and breadth of Poland.
My time, sir, is too limited to go into any detail with respect to this greatest of modern persecutions. Suffice it to say that humanity, truth and justice demand that this bestial policy of national extermination shall cease forthwith. Hon. members will no doubt be told that the reasons for these military visitations was merely to "pacify" the inhabitants of western Ukraine; but how the Nero of modern time, Marshal Pibudski, can justify the excesses of his debauched and degenerate soldiery is beyond all comprehension. For in the light of all that is human and ethical, in the light of our standards of what is right and just, this attempt by Poland to liquidate the Ukrainian question by means of physical torture and complete destruction of cultural and economic possessions, this attempt to divest by forceful means a minority of seven million Ukrainians of a natural and elemental attachment to their religion, language,

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Bennett
and culture, will go down in history as one of the mosit hideous, despicable, heinous and diabolical crimes ever perpetrated on a defenceless, peaceful and self-respecting people.
How can this house justify the murder of defenceless women and children? How can this house justify the wanton demolition of public and private property? In a word, how can this house justify the cunningly planned extermination of a whole race merely to gratify the insatiable and historical appetite for lust and rapacity of a ruling class that has always been stigmatized as the most reckless, dissipated, cruel and incompetent in Europe?
The world cannot expect the Ukrainians to sanction their own crucifixion; on the contrary it would be surprising if they did not use every effort to take the bleeding body of western Ukraine off the cross while life still exists and place it in the hands of a competent world physician for restoration to health and well being; for every race has the right to live according to its rights and traditions, and certainly no reasonable person will condemn the Ukrainians on this score for their unwillingness to commit national suicide.
The League of Nations has the necessary restorative powers if it only cares to exercise them. According to a treaty signed between Poland and the allied and associated powers, she was bound by guarantees to grant the Ukrainians equal political rights, local selfgovernment, and full freedom with regard to church matters, cultural, educational and economic development. These pledges and obligations were assented to and signed by the representatives of the Polish Government with a great flourish and with many promises to live up to them. But as soon as the Poles found themselves firmly entrenched in their domination of the whole country these same pledges and obligations were relegated to complete oblivion. In view therefore of the gravity of the situation and of the existence of a treaty binding Poland to certain minority guarantees, to which Canada was a signatory, I respectfully urge on behalf of three hundred thousand Ukranians resident in Canada that this matter be submitted to the council of the League of Nations in order that that body might institute an impartial inquiry by appointing a commission to investigate the whole situation in eastern Galicia, and take whatever steps it deems necessary to safeguard the rights of minorities in Poland.
