No doubt the house expects the government to make a statement at once with respect to a matter of this character. That
my hon. friend (Mr. Luchkovich) should bring the matter to the attention of this house, having regard to the fact that Canada is a member of the League of Nations and that, as he has told us, he himself has a personal interest in those concerned, is of course not surprising. But the extent to which this house may interfere or deal with such a question is an altogether different matter.
Years ago the parliament at Westminster considered alleged atrocities in Bulgaria and other parts of Europe. It has not been unusual at Westminster for members to discuss the treatment accorded by a country to certain classes of its citizens. In this country it is perhaps within the memory of all who have read the debates of the past that so eminent an authority as the Hon. Edward Blake, to say nothing of the Hon. John Costigan and others, thought that this house had full right and authority to pass resolutions with respect to Ireland. But in this instance Canada occupies a different relation to Poland and to other parts of the world from that which it did prior to the great war. Canada is a member of the League of Nations, and that being a tribunal in one sense, and having power to set up tribunals in another sense, which it has done, it would appear to me that all that can be done is to bring to the attention of that body, of which we are a member, the fact that certain representations have been made. It must be in the mind of every hon. member of this house that there are conflicting views as to what has transpired in Poland. On the one hand, the allegations to which my hon. friend has referred have been given wide publicity through the press and otherwise. On the other hand, Poland has been equally strong in her denials. Poland has declared that what was done was to stamp out incendiarism and various other offences in the communities affected. It is not for me, or, in my opinion, for this house to pass judgment upon the sufficiency of the evidence to establish either the charge, on the one hand, or the defence, on the other. But it might be important to direct attention to the fact that, in the very nature of things, it was to be expected that in the treaty of peace, when full regard was not had to self-determination in the sense in which that term was thought to be used by those in authority, some provision would be made safeguarding the rights of minorities. Accordingly, Article 8 of the treaty of Versailles, signed on July 28, 1919, provides that:
Polish nationals who belong to racial, religious or linguistic minorities shall enjoy the same treatment and security in law and in fact, as the other Polish nationals. And
1400	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Bennett
particularly they shall have equal right to establish, manage and control, at their own expense, charitable, religious and social institutions, schools and other educational establishments, with a right to use their own language and to use their religion freely therein.
That right, conceded to the minorities in what is now Poland, or the larger Poland that resulted from the military operations in eastern Galicia, is the basis oif the claim now made to the League of Nations.
There arises, then, the question as to how those rights may be protected by the League of Nations. And that question is one of very considerable difficulty. The truth is that no general system of jurisprudence has been established applicable where there are racial or linguistic or religious rights that are in any sense assailed or attacked. All that the league aims to do is to facilitate the solution of the problems that arise out of the existence of minorities in certain countries that enjoy the benefit of the provisions of treaties of peace and other treaties to which I might refer.
Now, the executive organ of 'the league is its council; and- the council of the league from time to time, when -cases are presented for its consideration, remits inquiries to committees or bodies of experts to make the necessary investigations. Petitions, of course, have been sent to the league from Canada, and large numbers of persons in this country have signed them. The hon. gentleman states that three hundred thousand Ukrainians in Canada are affected. These Canadians finding their kinsmen and relatives complaining of breach of the treaty, have of course appealed to the League of Nations to safeguard the rights, as they conceive them, oif their kinspeop'le in Poland. The -council has laid down certain rules with respect to petitions and1 their re-eeivability. These petitions:
(a)	Must have in view the protection of minorities in accordance with the treaties;
(b)	In particular, must not be submitted in the form of a request for the severance of political relations between the minority in question and the state of which it forms a part;
(c)	Must not emanate from an anonymous or unauthenticated source;
(d)	Must abstain from violent language;
(e)	Must contain information or refer to facts which have not recently been the subject of a petition submitted to the ordinary procedure.
These are the requirements with respect to oetitions. Now, from 1923 to 1930, it is idle to -deny t-ha-t there has been a great conflict in Poland between what you might call the Ukrainian nationalists and the Polish a-uthori-
[Mr. Bennett.l
ties; -and in 1930 the agitation reached a point which it had not previously touched. The results, as indicated by the Polish authorities and the Ukrainians, have -certainly been very contradictory. On the one hand, the Polish authorities say they have restored law and order and have stamped out in-cendiarism and offences of that kind. On the other hand the Ukrainians have represented, -as the hon. gentleman has just observed, that what -has happened is part of a campaign for the destruction of their nationality. On that state of facts it became necessary -for the -council -to take some action, -and so in -the end a -committee of inquiry was set up, which committee is now functioning, consisting of representatives of the United Kingdom, of Norway and of Italy. It has met twice during recent weeks and I understand will meet again before submitting its report to the sixty-third session of the council, which is to meet in Geneva on May 18. This committee is making the necessary inquiries to enable the council of the league to be seized of the facts and to determine what, if any, -action should be taken.
Under these circumstances I am sure the hon. gentleman will be the first to see that we in this parliament, of all places in the world-Canada being a member of the league -cannot take any action at this moment for by so doing we deny the authority of the very organization to which we belong, as we ourselves were parties to the setting up of the committee for the purpose of taking the action suggested. We cannot say that the committee will be ineffective or insufficient; we cannot, it seems to me, do more than support the council in any action it takes-it being a body of which we are a member-for the purpose of ascertaining the truth of the allegations made. I need hardly repeat that the Polish authorities have denied in very unequivocal language the accuracy and truthfulness of the charges made against them.
There is one other fact to which I think attention should be directed, and it is this: recently large numbers of petitions have been sent from this country to the league at Geneva. Recently one of the petitions was denied on the ground1 that the matters therein alleged had already been presented to the league and were now under consideration by the committee to which I referred. Within the last ten days the government has been advised that the petition forwarded by the Ukrainian Self Reliance League of Canada has been declared irreceiv-able because it contains no information not already included in seven petitions which are at present receiving the consideration of the

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Woodsworth
committee appointed at the last council in January to examine Ukrainian charges of treaty violations.
I think the hon. gentleman has discharged to the full his obligation and responsibility to those in Canada who are affected, and however strong may be his views, he must, and I think he will, like all of us, realize that this is not the tribunal which can hear the defence of those who are charged with these offences. That tribunal is one which we in common with other members of the league have set up to make a report upon the facts. When that report is made the council will take such action as may be necessary to enforce the claims of the minorities to the extent that their rights have been violated.
May I say in conclusion that the House of Commons of Canada has to be doubly careful to-day, more so than was necessary in days gone by. In the past we could readily make declarations touching upon and affecting the rights of peoples in other countries, but at the moment, having submitted to the jurisdiction of the League of Nations and having exercised with pride a very considerable influence in that body, we must in the vrny nature of things be careful that what we do does not reflect upon the action taken by a body of which we are a member, and especially in connection with a charge that one of our fellow members has failed to recognize its responsibilities. Our responsibility is to strive to see that such action is taken in the council as will protect the rights of minorities under a treaty which ensured their rights and, at the same time, to do so in such a way as not to oast discredit or suspicion upon the body known as the League of Nations, in which, as I have said, we are members and which is charged with responsibility under the treaties. It is for that reason I think we must speak with, shall I say moderation, and that all we Can usefully do is to press upon the council the necessity of taking such prompt action as will ensure the vindication of the rights of those who claim they have been deprived of the privileges to which they are entitled under the terms of the treaty. In doing that I am sure we will have the assistance and support of our fellow members in the league; for experience has shown, and the record of the proceedings of the league has indicated, that in every instance where a matter of this kind has been brought to the attention of the council and a committee has been appointed and a report made, it has not been slow or hesitant to take such action as the necessities of the case warrant.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some of
my Ukrainian friends asked me to support the proposal of the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Luchkovich). To this request I very gladly acceded because it seems to me that we have here a matter which is of such importance to a large number of our fellow Canadians that we cannot afford lightly to pass it by. I know there are some who will say:	Why should a matter of this kind be
discussed in the House of Commons? I think we have the best answer in the fact that we have in Canada some 300,000 Ukrain-ian-Canadians. Let me remind the committee that that number is almost four times the population of Prince Edward Island. Few people in eastern Canada recognize how important that population is to Canada and how necessary it is for us to see that they have no grievance.
There is a possibility that this discussion may tend to intensify the racial feeling which exists already between the Ukrainian and Polish communities in Canada. I recognize that danger, and anyone who has lived among the Ukrainians and Poles will recognize it also. Some have felt that we ought not to open this question, but in discussing this matter with my Polish friends-I have a number of Polish friends in Canada-as well as with my Ukrainian friends, I have tried to put it to them that after all the Polish people resident in Canada are not distinctly responsible for the acts of the Polish government and that, therefore, they should not take the matter in any personal way. I have taken the position that true patriotism does not consist in justifying the government of my country, "right or wrong." Last year I mentioned some of the atrocities which according to my information were being perpetrated in India, and some people rather resented the fact that I should mention those things in the house. Some of the newspapers were kind enough to suggest that I was anti-British and raised these questions because of some anti-British feeling. That is not so, because these matters are being freely discussed in the British papers. In England it is a matter of the policy of the British government and I take it I am a true Britisher when I try to remedy those things which I find to be evil. I do not take the ground that we in Canada have any special responsibility with regard to the conditions in India; but being members of the league, we are interested in a general way and we should assume our share of the responsibility In my judgment, we are truly patriotic when we seek to remedy any evils which may exist in our country or for which our governments may be responsible. I think my Polish friends in Can-
1402	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Woodsworth
ada will come to look at this matter in that way; for many of them are as deeply shocked as anyone else at what they read as to what is going on in the old country. In this connection I could not but think of what was said many years ago. Franklin asserted at one time: "Where liberty is, there is my home;" to which Thomas Paine replied: "Where liberty is not, there is my home." It seems to me that in our interrelated world every one of us is responsible to a certain degree for whatever goes on in any part of the world. That- is the situation which we are coming to realize more and more clearly. We cannot disregard our responsibilities toward humanity.
Let me urge, too. that in the house we should show an interest in our fellow Canadians of other races. We of Anglo-Saxon stock or we of Latin stock have our own particular problems. I think every Canadian must recognize that we of the English-speaking group ought to try more than we do to understand our fellow French-Canadians. I regret exceedingly it is difficult for some of us who are unable to speak French, especially those of us who are middle aged, to enter into the cultural life of our FrenchAIanadian fellow citizens.
But this is what I should like to impress upon the house, that long before we have developed a thorough-going understanding between the French and English portions of our community, we have had thrust upon us those other and exceedingly complicated problems which have arisen on account of the very large immigration to this country of peoples from various countries of Europe. If we are to succeed in incorporating these different peoples into our Canadian nationality, we shall have to try to the utmost to have a better understanding of them than most of us have at the present time. I wonder if I might refer to a book that has recently been published. I do this for the benefit of some Canadians *who may not know of it. It is entitled The Ukrainian Canadians, by Charles H. Young. Doctor Helen R. Y. Reid, of Montreal, in *writing a foreword to this book, says:
Finally the committee believes that a positive change of mind and attitude on the part of old Canadians towards the new Canadians is both due and necessary, not only for the unity of the country and for the development of a healthy Canadian spirit, but also for the promotion of international friendships and world peace. A racial study such as this which ve now offer would provide for a better understanding of the values, cultural and economic, contributed by each race to our Canadian civilization, and should, therefore, make for the establishment of better relations between the old and the new peoples of Canada.

I think, we have a really significant incident to-day when the hon. member for Vegreville, the first Ukrainian to sit in this Canadian house, comes to us and asks us to take up a matter which is of vital concern to that group from which he comes. This is an indication of a new condition into which we are emerging. It is an earnest of what may be possible in the future, that instead of these grievances being hidden away and talked about in secret, a prominent and well educated Canadian of Ukrainian stock can come into the House of Commons and from his seat present what he believes to be a matter of vital concern to the national group from which he comes.
Some of our Canadians I find take this attitude; let these people who come to us leave the old world behind. I confess sometimes I have a little bit of sympathy with the feeling that we should leave Europe behind and build up a new civilization on this North American continent. But I would point out that Britishers have not done that, and when the great war arose in Europe, tens of thousands of British born went back to their homes in order that they could, as they thought, defend the motherland. I would suggest that the man who forgets his fatherland and who is indifferent to the welfare of his own brothers and sisters will not make a very good Canadian citizen. We ought to bear that in mind. I have heard those who say: Let these people remember they are Canadians; let them forget the old country. Surely in this country we value men who do not forget the old, but rather bring with them the very best of the old. You cannot divest yourself of the old associations and traditions and be worth anything. The Englishman remembers the country from which he came; the Scotchman remembers the country whence he came. We value them because of that. The same thing is true with regard to Ukrainians or peoples of other nationalities who have thrown in their lot with us.
Let me say this with regard to these Ukrainians who have come to Canada: more than 10,000 of them voluntarily enlisted from western Canada at the time of the great war. If you talk of loyalty, that surely is an indication of loyalty to British institutions and as they conceived it and as most people did at that time; they were willing to answer the call which went forth. Just in passing, let me say I think it was one of the most disgraceful things that we on our part did not understand the situation, and while those
10,000	young men were enlisting, we deliberately disfranchised many of their fathers and

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Woodsworth
brothers. This just indicates the lack of knowledge and lack of sympathy that we have in regard to these newer Canadians. One of my Ukrainian friends said at the time; "You call us enemies of Breat Britain, we who are from Austria. Austria was an enemy of ours long before she was an enemy of Great Britain." I felt I could but hang my head in shame as I saw the way in which we misunderstood and mistreated these people. Not that we did it deliberately, but we did it ignorantly. Now the time has come when we shall have to take these racial and social questions more seriously.
Let me point out that if these matters in Europe are not settled on principles of justice, we are bound to have difficulties arising in this country because these old world difficulties will be reflected here. Out in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, there often occur community quarrels. Why? Simply because the Ukrainians are reading Ukrainian papers, the Poles are reading Polish papers, the Germans are reading German papers, and so on, and they are following in detail all these things that are happening in the old country. If peace and justice are not established in Europe, we shall have the same old battles fought out in this country. When we so readily accepted hundreds of thousands of immigrants from Europe, we did not know all the responsibilities which we were going to have to shoulder because of their coming here. The Europeans are here and we shall have to deal with the different problems which their coming presents.
Looking at the matter from a broader standpoint, I take it that we Canadians must come more and more to think internationally. The forefathers of most of us Canadians of the older stocks lived here before us for several generations in comparatively isolated communities. We were removed from the main world currents. But particularly since the war we have been drawn into those currents and when after the war Canada became a member of the League of Nations, we definitely took upon ourselves international responsibilities. I am not quite sure that the Prime Minister was correct in his statement with regard to what it was possible for us as a nation to do in this matter. Let me point out that according to the treaty, article 11:
It is also declared to be the friendly right of each member of the league to bring to the attention of the assembly or the council any circumstance whatever affecting international relations which threatens to disturb international peace or the good understanding between nations upon which peace depends.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure the hon.
member realizes that I am aware of that provision, but action has already been taken. The petitions having been presented and the committee set up, I said that we should not prejudge a matter that was sub judice.
The Prime Minister may be technically correct, but, after all, these petitions were presented .by private individuals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: By organizations, as well.

The petitions were presented by private organizations. I am not suggesting that we in this house can decide whether the charges made can be substantiated or not; but it does seem to me that we as a nation might make our representations to the League of Nations, either to the assembly or to the council. I think that that is a possibility under the clause which I have read.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They were made-in
January last-and the committee was set up in accordance with the representations.
But if I am rightly informed, they have been -made by private organizations, and not directly by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But Canada's representatives were a party to the representations. The petitions were submitted; some were received, some declined; and the committee was set up in consequence of the complaints made.

It may be that we have done all that we could. My submission would be that under clause 11 it is still competent for this house to take action and make representations with regard to this matter. Let me read one other clause of the Treaty of Peace. This will .be familiar to the Prime Minister, but perhaps not so familiar to all the members of the house. Article 23 reads:
Subject to and in accordance with the provisions of international conventions existing or hereafter to be agreed upon, the members of the league:
(a) will endeavour to secure and maintain fair and humane conditions of labour for men, women, and children, both in their own countries and in all countries to which their commercial and industrial relations extend, and for that purpose will establish and maintain the necessary international organizations.
So I take it that we are quite within our rights in taking any opportunity that we can of representing to any other nation any conditions which are liable to cause a breach of
1404	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Woodsworth
international peace, or of bringing to their attention any conditions which may bring hardship to any section of the community.
I am not going to follow the hon. member for Vegreville in any detail. I think he has shown that there is very good ground for believing that the rights of the minorities in Poland have been violated and that the treaty has been broken. Let me point out that, after all, Poland itself is more or less an arbitrary creation. The Poland that we have to-day is not the Poland that once existed, and I think that this new state is one of the big blunders of the peace treaty. We have set up a country with centralized powers, and we have relegated the minorities in that country to a very inferior position indeed. But aside from this, it seems to me that there is abundant evidence [DOT] to show that the treaty has not been strictly observed. I think there is a sort of presumptive evidence to that effect in the fact that there has been a great deal of difficulty experienced by other minorities in Poland. The members of the house may remember that the German minority have had trouble with the Polish government. Some months ago a committee was set up to deal with the charges brought by the German minority in Poland, and this was the report of the committee. I read from the "Monthly Summary of the League of Nations" for January, 1931, dealing with the sixty-second session of the council:
The Japanese representative, M. Yoshizawa, submitted a report on the position of the German minority in the Voivodies of Silesia, Poznan and Pomorze. The report, which was adopted by the council on January 24, 1931, reads as follows:
I shall make only two or three excerpts:
I should now like to consider the second element in the question, namely, that relating to the attacks alleged to have been made on the persons and property of members of the minority. The "Volksbund" petition gives a detailed account of 255 cases of this kind. I do not think I should now enter upon a detailed consideration of these cases. No one has denied that attacks of this kind took place, and that such attacks were sufficiently serious and widespread to justify the conclusion that there was in numerous eases an infringement of Article 75 and 83 of the Geneva Convention.
Then further:
As to direct responsibility-the Polish government has informed us that all the cases mentioned in the "Volksbund" petition have been the subject of thorough inquiry. We are told that as a result of those inquiries 125 cases were brought before the courts, that in 28 cases the public prosecutor of the republic instituted proceedings, and that in 10 of these the competent courts have already pronounced judgment. It is stated that disciplinary action has been taken against 17 officials.

Again:
Further, the council will desire to receive from the Polish government, before its next session, a complete and detailed statement of the results of the inquiries ordered in these different cases, and also of any penalties imposed and measures for compensation that may have been taken in consequence of these inquiries.
Again:
It is, in any case, essential that the German minority in the Voivodie of Silesia should regain that feeling of confidence which, unfortunately, seems to have been profoundly shaken, but without which it would be impossible to establish between the minority and the state that cooperation which, in the treaties and the resolutions of the assembly and the council of the League of Nations, constitutes a duty equally imperious for the state and for the minority concerned. The council will certainly desire to be informed in due time before its next session of any decisions which the Polish government may have felt right to take in this matter.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Vegreville, the trouble is that the Ukrainian people have no national home, they have ho great national state to back up their petitions, and so it is doubly incumbent on the other members of the league that they should take an active part in pushing forward this investigation.
It is not my desire to endeavour to substantiate in any way the charges which have already been made. Any hon. members who have read the Manchester Guardian must have noted the letters and articles which have been appearing in it for months. We are not so near the scene, of course, and we are not in so good a position to judge, but I note that a very large number of the members of the British House of Commons have taken an active interest in this matter. Among others I note the names of A. Fenner Brockway, Rhys Davies, Commander J. M. Kenworthy, Cecil Malone, M. Phillips Prince, Wilfred Wellock, and many other well-known members of the British house. With these statements before us, and with the information which has been brought to us to-day by the hon. member for Vegreville, we would be justified in taking whatever steps are possible. It may be that the Prime Minister is quite correct, and that all has been done under the machinery of the league that is now possible, but I would urge that the government itself should insist that there be no delay in making the fullest investigation possible.
Anyone who has been closely in touch with the Ukrainian community in Canada must realize that our Ukrainian citizens feel that this is a very, very important matter. It concerns the welfare of their brothers and sisters who are still living in Europe.

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Lapointe

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I trust that the hon. member heard my statement that the report of the committee was expected to be made to the council on the 18th day of May.

If I may interrupt, did I understand the Prime Minister to say that the committee of three was to investigate whether the petitions were correct according to the regulations set up by the league, or whether the committee was to make an investigation into the actual brutalities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The question of the
receivability of petitions is already provided for by regulations which I read, and the committee is making a report upon its investigations of the facts.

I desire to say one or two words in
connection with the protection of minorities. First may I say that the hon. member who has brought this matter to the attention of the house has made a most vigorous and able presentation, and the facts, if they are as he has described them, do not speak very highly for the present state of civilization. Of course, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has stated, there is another party to the difficulty, and that other party does not represent the facts in exactly the same light. However my hon. friend has said enough to justify the government's bringing the matter before the council of the League of Nations, pressing it and seeing that a proper investigation is made.
The matter of trouble in eastern Galicia first came to my attention in a rather strange manner, and I cannot resist the temptation to relate the incident. In 1922 I had the honour of being a member of the Canadian delegation to the League of Nations, accompanying the late Hon. Mr. Fielding. On the first day of the meetings of the assembly I received at the hotel a card on which were written the names of three men who represented themselves to be delegates from eastern Galicia. They were shown to my room, and before Mr. Fielding and myself they pleaded their case very eloquently. Two of them spoke neither French or English, but one spoke very good French and fairly good English. After we had discussed the matter with them for some time and had undertaken to discuss it with other British delegates, the one who had been speaking addressed me as follows: "Does not Your Excellency remember me?" Hon. members should take note of the fact that in Europe all ministers are called "your excellency." In a most humble 22110-90
way I replied, "Have I ever seen you before?" He said, "When Your Excellency was in his last year at the classical college of Rimouski I was in my first year." "Well," I said, "you are from Rimouski?" He said, "My name is Jean, and I was bom in St. Simon de Rimouski." I said, "If your name is Jean and you were born in St. Simon de Rimouski, drop the 'Excellency' at once." He happened to be a young priest who was completing his education in Europe when the war broke out. He was in Galicia at the time and, having to remain there, had become one of the leaders of the nation. I believe that incident tends to show that Canadians can be successful everywhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What was his nationality?

French-Canadian. He
is now in the Abitibi district in the province of Quebec, and he has brought with him a great many of those Galician people who indeed are industrious settlers within our province.
The question of the treatment of minorities is a troublesome one and presents one of the greatest difficulties with which the League of Nations has to deal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

And it could not be
otherwise. Following the war many new countries were formed; they were carved out of the territories formerly included in other countries and inevitably there came together people of various races differing in language and religion. Necessarily difficulties were bound to arise. Those who attended the peace conference and those who were responsible for the various peace 'treaties knew that such difficulties would arise and they took good care to ensure a protection for linguistic, racial and religious minorities in those various countries. The same clause may be seen in all the treaties concerning Austria, Hungary, Roumania, Poland, Bulgaria, Greece and other countries.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	And the British North
America Act.

Yes, I may say a word
about that at a later time. It was considered that the fundamental principle of protection for minorities was of international concern, and the guarantee was entrusted to the League of Nations. I am not sure that I properly understood my right hon. friend but I thought he said the league had not, except in a very mild manner, the authority to intervene.

1408	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Lapointe

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I said the council was
the instrument set up by the league. The league itself has very limited powers to enforce the conclusion at which they might arrive after inquiries had been made. That is what I endeavoured to say.
The league is authorized to take any steps it may deem proper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

I agree, however, with
my right hon. friend that steps might be taken which might not always be opportune.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so.

The work of the league
in that matter must be a work of conciliation, otherwise it could not achieve results; its work would be nullified by the obstructive tactics of the government affected. A state or a government cannot be coerced in a matter of that kind. Of course, conciliation, education, and negotiation can always be resorted to, and, I believe, especially in these modern times those 'are the only practical ways of achieving results in respect to such matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And the weight of public opinion.

Yes, the weight of public opinion; I agree with my right hon. friend in that suggestion. I wish to describe particularly the rights of minorities under the treaty. For instance the treaties laid down:

that nationals belonging to minorities shall have an equal right to establish, manage and control at their own expense charitable, religious and social institutions, schools and other educational establishments, with the right to use their own language, and to exercise their religion freely therein.
And, further:
The obligation to grant adequate facilities in towns and districts where there is a considerable proportion of nationals speaking a language other than the official language of the state, to ensure that in the primary schools (1) the instruction shall be given to the children of such nationals through the medium of their own language.
Then there is another clause which might be of special interest in a certain part of this country. It is said:
The treaties also lay down that in towns and districts where there is a considerable proportion of nationals of the country belonging to racial, religious or linguistic minorities, these minorities shall be assured an equitable share in the enjoyment and application of the sums which may be provided out of public funds under the state, municipal or other budget, for educational, religious or charitable purposes.

Mr. LaVERGNE: Even when that minority is a majority in the district.

Exactly. The league has established, as occasion arose, minority committees, such as the one the right hon. gentleman has referred to, but apparently-and this may be the trouble of my hon. friend and his friends-their proceedings are kept secret. I remember having heard Sir Austen Chamberlain say that it was in the interests of the negotiations and of a settlement that the proceedings of the committee should be kept secret. On the other hand, the public at large cannot see what is the proportion of successes and reverses in the negotiations of those committees. I read somewhere that there have been three hundred applications from minorities and about one hundred and fifty investigations. I think at the last assembly, or the last but one, the suggestion was made-and there is a strong current of opinion behind it-that there should be a permanent commission dealing with those problems instead of roving committees, which are not stable in their character because it happens very often that the members do not attend and are represented by substitutes.
Now, there is another matter that I wish to mention. There are minorities elsewhere than in those countries which have come into existence by the treaties of peace, and on September 21, 1922, the League of Nations passed a resolution which I wish to call to the attention of the house. I remember Roumania, for instance, saying to the assembly: "Why should we be treated because we have treaties of this kind in a different manner from the other countries of the. world who are forcing us to observe the treaty clauses?" This is the resolution:
The assembly expresses the hope that the states which are not bound by any legal obligations to the league with respect to minorities will nevertheless observe in the treatment of their own racial, religious, or linguistic minorities at least as high a standard of justice and toleration as is required by any of the treaties and by the regular action of the council.
I think that was a very proper resolution to adopt. Even since that time there have been proposals to the effect that all the members of the Society of the League of Nations should have a treaty under which they would accept the clauses protecting the minorities in their respective territories. Those proposals are still before the league, which has not yet taken action, but some objectors represented that it might 'be very well to apply those clauses to minorities which have passed under another flag as a result of war or of diplomatic negotiations, but not to groups

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. LaVergne
which might settle in a country of their own free will, and which necessarily must adopt the customs and the usages of that country.

Yes. In this country, on various occasions we have had difficulties with regard to minorities concerning school and language. I wish to emphasize this remark which I have already made, that the French minority in Canada is of course composed of citizens who are loyal to the crown, who are proud and happy to be as they are to-day, but who have come under the British flag not of their own free will but as the result of wars of long duration, negotiations and treaties. Therefore I do not see why they should be treated differently from those various peoples in central Europe that have come into other nations by the peace treaties following the late war. The French in Canada have always represented that they have the right to their language, that they were the first settlers in the country, that they are at home everywhere in Canada; and certainly they resent any attempt, for instance to deprive their children of receiving education in their mother tongue. But even there, as is the case with regard to the treatment of minorities in the League of Nations, I know that coercive methods cannot serve any useful purpose.	It is through conciliation,
negotiation, weight of public opinion that this right-not privilege-can be successfully recognized and granted everywhere. Consequently when a member of this government finds it his duty to refer to a serious educational and language trouble in one province, certainly there is good ground for thinking it is a case where some arrangement could be made.
I repeat, I am in favour of the motion of my hon. friend-if it can be called a motion- that the weight of Canada's prestige and Canada's authority should be behind the move advocated by my hon. friend and that a full investigation should be made by the League of Nations. But after all we must set our own house in order everywhere in this country. We in Canada are members of the League of Nations, as we are in Eurpoe, and I think every one of the various parts of Canada should set an example to those nations to whom we preach moderation and justice.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny): Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any length. I rise to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) on his remarks. I am glad to find that, companions at university, we are still very close 22U0- 90.}
together in our older age. I think the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) was quite right in bringing this question before the house. Brought up to regard Poland as having been for so many centuries the soldier of Christianity, I must confess that it is a sort of heart-break to me to learn of the things that are going on there; and I agree with the hon. member for Quebec East that the prestige of Canada should be behind the claim of the Ukrainian people in this country for justice in the matter. But, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has said, inasmuch as the machinery already exists nothing can be done except for this parliament to pass a resolution asking for justice, as was done in days gone by when Ireland was in sorrow. There again, however, I agree with the hon. member for Quebec East. If we wish to instruct other nations in their duty in the way of justice to minorities, we should first put our own house in order; and we need not cross the seas, to Poland or Roumania, to find minorities that are suffering. We need not step out of our own country. To tell the truth, outside the province of Quebec, every minority in every province of Canada has suffered. Our position would be a rather sad one if we undertook to teach other peoples before settling our own troubles. As the hon. member for Quebec East has said, it is only by agitating and calling for justice, not by coercion, that we can settle this question.
Before concluding, I might say this. The dual civilization of Canada is the greatest gift Providence has ever bestowed upon any country in the world, and we must maintain it. And if I were an English-speaking Canadian I should be the first one to insist upon the maintenance of that dual civilization, because therein we find a guarantee for the preservation of our country. Therein lies the differentiation of Canada from the United States-our greatest safeguard for the maintenance in Canada of British institutions and the preservation of this Dominion from what, to my mind, is its greatest menace, namely, absorption in the melting pot of America.

subtopic: BILL TO OBVIATE NECESSITY OF REELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
In that case, may I submit that the alteration asked for by the hon. gentleman in his bill is that we should do away with an almost prehistoric piece of legislation dating back to the days of good Queen Anne. At that time there was a tremendous conflict between the commons and the crown, and it was the desire to prevent the continued usurpation by the crown of the powers of the commons that induced the enactment of the legislation which in its present form compels any individual member of the House of Commons selected for a portfolio to return to the electorate in his constituency or in some other constituency for reelection. No one knows better than the present leader of the government (Mr. Bennett) the difficulties entailed in this procedure. I have distinct recollection of instances during my short life in parliament where the best man available within the party was not elected for office because a majority in his constituency could not be ensured, and such has been the experience in all British parliaments. It is exceedingly unfair to a minister himself, very often a man of humble means, to be compelled to meet the expenses of an election even though at the time he be a member of the House of Commons. The point I would make in this connection is that no man whose ability commends him to the office should be passed over simply because his seat does not appear to be a safe one. If his abilities are such or promise to be such as to justify the appointment, that and that alone should be the sole consideration. It is unfair to the electors in the constituency to subject them to the disturbance of a byelection, especially if it comes shortly after the general elections. The only ones that could be interested in those performances would be the opposition.
Another reason which makes the present system unfair is that the person selected is diverted from his duties for the three or four weeks necessary to carry on an election at the very time he should be acquainting him-

self with those duties and familiarizing himself, in the case of many of the portfolios, with the tremendous work entailed in carrying them out. Moreover, in by-elections of this character it frequently happens that the person nominated to the portfolio is subjected to all sorts of pressure and induced to make many statements he would not otherwise make were he in office for some time studying its responsibilities and securing the well-developed advice of his colleagues.
Speaking on this very question in the British house, I think in 1926, Sir John Simon contended that perhaps one of the most serious aspects of the legislation in this respect was that very often a newly appointed minister during the period1 of such by-election forgot for the time being that he was no longer a pi'ivate individual and frequently gave voice to expressions regarding government policies that afterwards required denial on .the part of the ministry involved. That would be a most embarrassing situation for all parties.
A measure of this character would be of much greater value to a ministry with a small majority than to a ministry such as we have now facing us. For example, had this proposed legislation been on the statute book in 1926-I have no doubt the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) will raise this point-the ministry of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, had it so desired, might have retained office, constitutionally at least, for the continuation of the term of that parliament, whereas on account of the unconstitutional and illegal position in which they found themselves they were rejected by the house and compelled to go prematurely to the country. So far as we in this corner of the house were concerned, the result was that we lost at least one year in having brought into force certain legislation which at that time was exceedingly desirable. I refer specifically to the question of the revaluation of soldier settlers' land, and also to other measures such as the Long Term Farm Loans Act.
The present method, as is stated by Sir William Anson in his Law and Custom of the Constitution, causes needless and vexatious delay in the conduct of public business. It distracts the mind of the member selected for a cabinet position from the duties of his office and very frequently embroils the entire ministry in the particular by-election. I think hon. members will concede that all elections are annoying. If I were asked for my own choice in the matter, I would say that the most satisfactory condition of affairs would be one where the present personnel sat forever and simply swapped positions at the will of the

Ministers of the Crown
House of Commons. However, it is not likely that such a condition will come in my time, so I am compelled to accept the situation as it is and do the best I can to carry on.
I am willing to concede another objection which may be taken to this measure. There is no doubt in my mind-and I say this with all respect-that the present ministry even after the short time it has been in office could hardly expect to go back to the country today and be returned in anything like its present strength. We have not in the house at the present time a minister of labour, and sooner or later the present administration will in all probability be compelled to select such a minister. Should this bill be enacted at the present session and become operative immediately thereafter, it is quite possible that the new minister of labour would not have to submit himself to the electorate, and therefore the public would be denied an opportunity of expressing an opinion upon the present administration. To offset that argument, which is a valid one, I submit that it is very rarely that by means of a by-election of the kind which would likely follow such an appointment any fair estimate of the general opinion of the public can be secured, because the person selected would no doubt contest a seat which from the experience of history it was felt would give a majority to the Conservative member seeking reelection on acceptance of the portfolio.
The one great objection which could be offered to this bill is one -which has been raised in other times, namely that its effect would be to deny to the electorate the power to give expression to its resentment against the type of administration which was then in office. But I submit that as our parliamentary term is only four years, sometimes not more than three, no great hardship will result; as a matter of fact in each constituency it frequently happens that local issues predominate and overshadow the issues concerning the general welfare of the nation. If it is contended, then, that the electorate would by such legislation as this be denied the power of expressing its dislike for an administration, I submit the only remedy would be to offer an election to the entire country and ask all of Canada to decide upon the minister's appointment. That, of course, would be absurd, and an utterly unnecessary expense. I think that disposes of one criticism that I can foresee against this legislation.
The present situation with regard to the Prime Minister himself is interesting. If the present Prime Minister of Canada desires to assume, as possibly he might, some further portfolios, under the present law as I read
it he would have to go to the country on the assumption of each of them. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) assures me that this is not the case. It was the case in Britain prior to 1926. In 1919 the first attempt was made in the British house to amend this legislation. At that time I think it was the Right Hon. Bonar Law who introduced the proposed amendment, which was in much the same form as the bill now before the house, the purpose being to amend the then existing legislation so as to provide that no member of the House of Commons, on being appointed to the ministry, need appeal again to the electorate. In the committee stage an amendment was introduced to the bill, providing that this should not apply after the administration had held office for nine months. I submit in this connection that nine months have elapsed since the election of the present administration bo office, and there would be little advantage in introducing the legislation unless it were to apply solely to subsequent parliaments, or to whatever by-elections might bake place in the next few years. Mr. Bonar Law, however, in accepting the amendment, used that expression which has since become a famous quotation:
Perhaps it is preferable to take two bites at a cherry. We will take the first bite now, and the second later.
The second and complete bite was taken in 1926 when the necessary change was again introduced into the British house, and I understand it passed at that time by a very large majority. The situation then was that the Conservative party in the British house had an enormous majority. The situation in Canada is that the Conservative party in this house has an enormous majority. But at that time Sir John Simon, I think it was, used this expression:
The position here is not as it is at the moment in Canada, where a ministry is poised on so narrow a ledge that considerations which are not necessarily consideration of the first order may have to determine exactly how to choose this colleague or how to refuse that.
Now the situation- -is reversed; in this country we have a Conservative government in power with a very large majority, whereas in the British house there is in power a Labour party tottering on the brink of compromise on every occasion.
Some extremists in -the house may point out that legislation of this kind would simply give to the executive powers or privileges that in the past we took from the crown. I am inclined at times to agree with those who criticize the present form of parliamentary government in this and other countries because of the tremendous and growing
Ministers of the Crown

power of the executive council. I cannot, however, see that the enactment of the legislation now proposed would necessarily in any way add to their powers in this house. What it would do in effect would be to remove from this country an anomalous and almost prehistoric condition that so unnecessarily hampers business and increases the cost of administration. Another hon. gentleman pointed out at one time that it would remove the only effective check over the executive by the electorate. I have dealt with that already. I do not think by-elections have ever been sufficiently intelligently conducted under existing conditions to bring into the light, as they would be brought in a general election, all the major issues facing the whole country; but they are decided for the most part on local issues.
I commend the legislation to the consideration of the house. I ask the house to give the bill its second reading, in the hope that it may be referred to the committee on privileges and elections. I hope the hon. member for Oartier will not condemn me too much if I do what I think he would do as a reasonable member of the house under the same conditions. I am not going to insist on the measure passing in its present actual form, but like Bonar Law I would be willing to take two bites of a cherry. If the time limitation were brought in the legislation could be introduced at once, in which case whoever becomes Minister of Labour in this house would have to submit himself to the electorate; thereupon the administration might receive a severe shock; on the other hand, it night not. I do not think any definite conclusion could be drawn from an election under those conditions.
The clauses of the bill are simple. All they do is modify the existing legislation in the direction I have indicated. The matter has received consideration in many parliaments other than ours. It is already, as I have indicated, enacted in the British house. It was enacted in New South Wales parliament in 1906. It has been in force in South Australia and New Zealand since the inception. It is also in force in Tasmania and in Queensland. The Union of South Africa like the Commonwealth of Australia, and the Irish Free State, have had it since the new constitution came into force. I ask the house to let the bill pass its second reading and then go, I hope, to the committee on privileges and elections.

speechtext:
I quite accept my hon. friend's word. I hope that he will be equally prepared to accept mine when I say that when on more than one occasion the same hon. member introduced this measure when I was sitting on the other side of the

Ministers oj the Crown
house and when the iparty which I have the honour to lead was in office, discussing the measure together we repeatedly argued the point as to whether it would be in the public interest in a democratic country to take away from the electorate the right it now has of voicing its opinion in the manner which is afforded by a by-election, where a minister of the crown is being appointed to office for the first time. The argument, as I remember it, of my hon. friend was always to the effect that it was an absurdity for a by-election to be necessitated immediately after a government had been returned to office or during a certain period of time thereafter, but that there might be reasons why by-elections should continue to take place when ministers of the crown were appointed at some period of time considerably beyond that at which a ministry itself had taken office. However, whether that is his view or not, I should like as one member, on the second reading of the bill to say that it is the view that in the interests of the electorate of this country I myself entertain. I favour the idea of allowing a ministry, after it has been returned to office at a general election, to have its ministers returned by acclamation if they have been elected as members of the house. When hon. gentlemen opposite were elected there was no opposition put to the return of any of their members as ministers of the crown. Indeed, so far as the official opposition was concerned, we did not limit our withholding of opposition to members of the administration who had been returned to the House of Commons, but when the /present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) sought a seat elsewhere, so far as the opposition had a voice in the matter at all, it was used in persuading those in the constituency in which he ran not to oppose him but to allow him to be returned by acclamation, which he was. I think that a practice of this kind, where a new ministry is formed immediately after a general election out of members elected to parliament, is a good one to follow, but I think that there should be a limit of time within which the practice should apply. That limit originally in the case of Great Britain was nine months. I should think we might do well to follow the British practice, proceeding by stages. If we are to change our practice in Canada, let us do it step by step as was done in Great Britain, and amend this measure so as to make the new provision applicable to members of a ministry which has just been returned and to ministers who may seek reelection within a period of nine months thereafter. I do submit that there are very strong reasons
from the point of view of the ministry itself as well as from the point of view of the general public, why by-elections should take place where ministers who have not theretofore held office are brought into a government, especially where a government has been in power from one to two or three or four years.
The limit of opportunity of appealing to an electorate is fixed by statute at a period of five years. It might well be that within that period of time the public itself would wish to voice its opinion in regard to policies which have developed in the course of time during which the ministry has held office. Every by-election affords that opportunity to a degree and there is a special reason why that opportunity should be given where a ministry undertakes to change its complexion without having consulted the electorate in the first instance.
Then with respect to a minister himself, a minister of the crown has a responsibility very much greater than that of a private member of parliament. A member has a very special responsibility the moment he becomes a minister of the crown. An electorate may be prepared to support an hon. member of the house as a member of the commons, where the same electorate might not be prepared to entrust him with the additional responsibility that attaches to a minister of the crown holding a particular portfolio. I am saying that not in the way of reflection upon anyone who may be taken into a ministry at any time, but I say that it is one of those many safeguards which in the interests of the public generally it seems to me wise to throw around the office of a responsible minister of the crown and which I believe it is also wise to throw around whoever may be called upon to fill such a position. I am prepared to agree to the general principle of the bill, though limiting its main provision to a period of time; I shall not oppose the second reading. I hope the house will feel that in the absence of the sponsor of the bill, it might remain at that stage and that it will not be necessary to proceed in committee on its provisions this evening.

This bill is really an innovation, and if passed would change a practice which has been in effect in Canada since confederation. When a similar bill was before the British House of Commons it was argued by some hon. members that the fact the British constitution could be amended showed its value.
There are many arguments which could be used for and against the proposal embodied in the bill. Mr. Dunnico, speaking in the British House of Commons, used the following argument against a similar bill introduced into that house:
Suppose a minister resigns because he feels he is not getting enough money to carry on his department, would it be right for the Prime Minister to put a man in his place without consulting the people?
That is one argument which was used against the change then proposed in Great Britain. Mr. Dunnico said that the bill involved an infringement on the rights of the electorate and a departure from the principles of democracy. He claimed that with all its faults and shortcomings, democracy would

Up to the moment that my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) proposed his amendment I was inclined to feel a certain sympathy with him in the suggestions that this measure be not pressed unduly just at present. The amendment however does give to the action of the government a significance which I doubt very much the government has fully appreciated. The situation at the moment is this. There are in the district of Patricia six hundred people who have not the right to vote at a general election in Canada or in a by-election in the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River; they are disfranchised. A member of the government now introduces an amendment to this motion Which may make it impossible, no matter what circumstances may arise, to consider the inclusion of these six hundred persons as electors for that particular constituency should there be occasion within a certain period of time for any reason to consult the people in that riding.
I remember quite well the circumstances that occasioned the postponement of this bill at the time it was originally introduced by the present sponsor, the then Minister of Labour. We were just on the eve of a general election and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), speaking then as leader of the opposition, maintained very strongly that there was no part of Ontario where the people had not the right to vote. He said that there was no group of electors in Ontario who were not included in some federal constituency. That was the position he took, and he so advised the house. In that statement he was entirely in the wrong, for there were in the district of Patricia six hundred persons who had been included in the constituency under the Ontario Electoral Act and who had the right to vote in a provincial election, but who were not included in any federal constituency. The boundaries of the constituency as fixed for provincial purposes were narrower than those fixed for Dominion elections. There was not at the time opportunity to go carefully into the matter. The hon. member took the matter up at once at the next session and is now bringing it up again. The purpose of this bill as introduced by the former Minister of Labour, is like its predecessors, to make the boundaries of the
fMr. Stevens.]
federal district as terminous with the boundaries of the provincial district: in other words, to give all the people duly qualified in that Patricia area the right to vote in federal as well as in provincial elections. It was because of the immediate pressure of prorogation that the bill was not proceeded with before the general election of 1930 and as I have said it was not proceeded with largely because of representations which were made at that time by the then leader of the opposition.
I have in my hand a statement from the chief electoral officer submitted to the Hon. Lucien Cannon, at that time Solicitor General. It reads:
Ottawa, May 29, 1930.
In the Representation Act of 1924 the district of Patricia has not been included in any electoral district of the province of Ontario or of any other province. Therefore persons residing in the district of Patricia, which is situated north of the English river, are not entitled to vote at a Dominion election.
Jules Castonguay,
Chief Electoral Officer.
That means that there are at the present time at least six hundred persons who are disfranchised, and the amendment now proposes to make doubly sure that they shall so remain That surely is not in accordance with representative institutions; and whatever may be done with the bill, for reasons which may have to do with the census which is to be taken, I do submit that this house should not in the interval, seek deliberately, by a motion of the government to disfranchise six hundred electors in the district in question.

I
congratulate the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) on the splendid presentation of his case to-day. We who form a part of any minority in Canada can easily extend our sympathies to minorities in other parts of the world, and certainly I can say this for myself, having lived in a section of Canada where the minority rights of Freneh-Canadians have been taken away one at a time. Knowing how the French-Canadians have been deprived of these rights, and realizing that this has retarded the progress of those parts of Canada where such rights have been denied the people, we can readily sympathize with any minority, wherever it may be.
Some controversy has taken place with regard to the atrocities alleged to have been committed in Poland. I have received a copy of a book entitled Ukraine-The Sorest Spot Of Europe, issued by the Ukraine Information Bureau. If the facts as related in this book are true, I feel certain that the best element in Poland, knowing them as I do in this country, would be the first to ask for redress. I received another book entitled Polish Library Of Facts-The Situation In Southeastern Poland ("Eastern Galicia"), published by the American-Polish Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Incorporated, in New York city, in which are refuted the statements
made in the other publication. The facts could be very easily ascertained, Canada, being a member of the League of Nations and a signatory to the treaty of Versailles, and having guaranteed protection to the minorities in certain component parts of Europe, should make every effort to discover the truth, and if such atrocities as have been described are being committed, do everything in her power to have them stopped.
The Ukrainian is a fine law-abiding citizen who has made a great contribution to this country, especially to western Canada. He is a good living citizen, the equal of any who come from other countries in central Europe. This matter should be investigated and I am glad the hon. member has brought it to the attention of the committee. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) Secretary of State for External Affairs will do everything in his power to see that tho League of Nations takes note of this debate.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) has covered the subject matter of this debate so well that there is very little left to be added thereto. However, I intend to review briefly the history of this people from early times. From the dawn of history there has been a Ukrainian race, with its own language, its own culture and its own literature, antedating the Norman conquest of England. For ages the Ukraine was the battle ground of the east and west, between oriental and occidental, between Mohammedanism and Christianity, and it bore the brunt of saving Europe, of saving Christianity from Mohammedanism and from the Turks and Tartars. It was the King of Poland, John Sobieski, who drove the Turk and Tartar out of Vienna and saved Europe from Mohammedanism, and his army was composed largely of Ukrainian cossacks.
The province of East Galicia, which is under discussion at this time, is only a part of the Ukraine, the larger portion, as we know, being incorporated in Soviet Russia. In 1654 this particular part of the Ukraine was ceded to Poland by Russia. On the dismemberment of Poland in 1772 this' province fell to Austria and it was, as we know it now, the province of East Galicia in Austria. On the breaking up of Austria after the great war this state declared itself independent under the name of West Ukraine, but it had to fight Soviet Russia on the one hand and Poland on the other, and the state never had an opportunity to exist; it never enjoyed peace long enough to build up a government or to do anything for itself. Austria surrendered all rights and
1418	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Campbell
interests in East Galicia to the allied powers under the treaty of St. Germain which was signed on September 10, 1919. The allied powers, including Great Britain, by the acceptance of that treaty became legally and morally responsible for the well-being of the people in that territory. On December 8, 1919, the supreme council of the peace conference laid out the boundary between West Ukraine and Poland, known as the Curzon line, which formed the boundary line between the states of West Ukraine and Poland. The very fact that that boundary was drawn up by the supreme council of the peace conference showed that the purpose was to give to that state self-determination; at any rate it was shown clearly that it was not the purpose to leave it under Polish domination. United States Secretary of State Colby issued a statement to the press on October 10, 1920, in which he stated that Poland must be an ethnographic state and nothing more, and that she must accept the Curzon line as her eastern boundary. This clearly proves that the allied nations had some responsibility in guaranteeing these people their self determination. However, in spite of the legal position in 1919 Poland forcibly took possession of the country and has held it ever since. May I quote briefly from an editorial which appeared in the Manchester Guardian of March 15, last, which reads in part:
When the Austro-Hungarian empire foundered the Ukrainians, like the Poles, the Czechs, and the Croats, proclaimed their independence in accordance with the principle of selfdetermination championed by President Wilson and by the allies, and, like the others, they fought to defend their newly asserted independence. But in June, 1919, the supreme council allowed the Poles to continue to occupy the western Ukraine, though expressly^ reserving the ultimate status of that region for future settlement.
I do not think I need refer to the treaty of minorities, as the Prime Minister referred to that matter this afternoon and the hon. member for Vegreville has covered it very well. This treaty was signed on June 28, 1919, between Poland on the one hand and the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy and Japan on the other and guaranteed full rights of nationality, language, race, religion and so on to all non-Polish races in the new Polish state. From that I would like to quote part of article 12, which reads:
Poland agrees that any member of the council of the League of Nations shall have the right to bring to the attention of the council any infraction, or any danger of infraction, of any of these obligations, and that the council may thereupon take such action and give such direction as it may deem proper and effective in the circumstances.

This has a very direct application to Canada, because Canada is a member of the League of Nations and the action that it is proposed to take to-day is taken, I presume, under that clause.
It is not necessary for me to deal with the question of the alleged' atrocities, 'because that has been very well covered by the hon. member for Vegreville. The question is of vital interest to at least one third of a million of Canadian citizens of Ukrainian stock. That fact in itself is entitled to some consideration outside altogether of the humanitarian angle of the question and Canada's responsibility as a member of the League of Nations. The request that Canada as a member of the league should support an independent investigation into this question and let the world know the actual conditions, seems to me a very modest one.
This afternoon the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) mentioned that a committee was already dealing with this matter. I am not entirely clear about that. If I am wrong, perhaps the Prime Minister can set me right. My understanding is that that committee is dealing simply with the petitions; that is, that committee is not appointed to go into Poland and to make a thorough examination and investigation. If it is, of course the matter has gone as far as we can go now, but my understanding is as I have indicated.

I tried to make that clear this afternoon.

I quite appreciate that. I was not dear on that point. My understanding was that the committee was circumscribed in its powers, and was dealing only with the subject matter of the petitions. What the Prime Minister has stated, however, would seem to clear the matter up to some, extent, and we hope this investigation will have some good results.

It
is not my intention to prolong the discussion; I desire simply to say a few words of approval of the presentation of the case by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich). The Ukrainian people in Canada have made
