good citizens. Three hundred thousand of them have come out to this country, most of them to western Canada, and the younger generation have certainly taken on their Canadian citizenship in a very commendable manner. I know many of them intimately and consequently I cannot help feeling a good deal of sympathy towards them in their case.
The League of Nations, as I understand the matter, have set down certain very definite principles dealing with questions of the rights of minorities. There is no doubt that the Ukrainian minority in Poland has certain definite rights. Those, I understand, according to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) this afternoon, are now under the definite consideration of the League of Nations and will be investigated. Canada has already selected her delegates who will go there with a knowledge of the situation so far as the Canadian people and parliament are concerned. The rights of the Ukrainian minority will be respected and looked after.
Canada is in a peculiar position in regard to the question of the rights of minorities. The soul of Canadian history and progress rests, I believe, to a large extent upon the manner in which the Canadian people have treated their minorities. Those rights have been respected from the earliest days of Canadian history extending down to more recent days, and particularly as applied to the very people of whom we are speaking, when they came out to Canada as a minority and became Canadian citizens.
It is not my intention to deal with this matter at any greater length. I simply wish to express in these few words my approval of the presentation of the matter by the hon. member for Vegreville, and also of the action taken by the Canadian government in respect to its representation at the League of Nations.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton):
speechtext:
I have no intention of trespassing upon the time of the committee for more than a very few minutes. I am glad that the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) brought this subject to the attention of the committee for discussion and debate. I am glad, for two reasons, that he did so; first, because it afforded an occasion for the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to make to the house and to the country the statement he made this afternoon as to the present position of this question; in the next place it has given an opportunity to hon. members in all parts of the chamber, representing all sections of political thought, to show that we are of one mind in our attitude on this matter. After all, as the Prime Minister stated this afternoon, the only
sanction which international law possesses is the sanction of public opinion, and the more clear, emphatic and insistent public opinion is upon any question of international interest, the greater will be the effective power of those principles of international law which are involved. In no way can the public opinion of this nation better express itself than through the opinion of this house, especially when it is shared so largely by all political sections represented here.
I have no intention of going into the history of the Ukrainian people or the question of the rights of minorities. I shall do no more than deal for a few minutes with the specific matter that has been brought before the committee.
I am not concerned with the wisdom or the unwisdom of the action of the Paris peace conference in dividing up amongst four nations the Ukrainian people and the land which they inhabit. I shall not discuss the question whether the charges which are made and which we have heard to-day are true or untrue. We cannot in that matter arrogate to ourselves the place or the powers or the functions of a judge. For the most part, if not entirely so, the evidence that is brought before us, at least so far as the great majority of hon. members of the house are concerned, is hearsay. It is true that the volume of the evidence, the nature of the authority, the seriousness of the charges, and the sources from which they come, are such as to make it imperative that some action be taken, and I am perfectly certain that the house and the country will accept the statement made by the Prime Minister that action has been taken. As I understand the suggestions of the hon. member for Vegreville, all he had in mind was to call attention to the conditions and to insist that, they required some action, some investigation, without saying whether we believe the charges to be true or false. We are not in a position to say whether they are true or whether they are false. But we have a right, I think, to ask for such action, for the sake not merely of the Ukrainian people themselves but also of the Polish nation and the Polish government, whose reputation and good name have been called in question. If the charges are true, they should be proved to be true; if they are false they should be silenced. That is all we ask.
Action should be taken also for the sake of the League of Nations itself. A great many people in Canada and throughout the world regarded the institution of the League of Nations as a more or less utopian idea. They never conceived that it would be possible for the League of Nations to bring about any real
1420	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Bury
results in the way of pacification or the settlement of great international questions and problems that might be the cause of war. But history has shown that the League of Nations is a practical force, not a mere utopian dream. For the sake of its own reputation and its own effectiveness, for the sake of the hopes that were based upon it when it was brought into being and the hopes that are still harboured in the breasts of people who have faith in its efficiency, it is essential that the League of Nations take action, and I have no doubt that it will do so. No aspersion is cast upon the Polish people by the house, by the people of Canada, or iby any of those who support the address of the hon. member for Veg-reville. The Polish people themselves say that the charges are not true, and they ask that an investigation shall be made. We are simply taking them at their word. We are only saying that even for their own sake everything should be made absolutely clear; that if the charges are false they should be proved false; that if they are true, then, for the sake of the good name of Poland itself, action should be taken to put an end to that which has occasioned them. That is the position I believe which most members of the house take. That is the position whieh I myself take.
I have in my hand a letter from the bishop of the Ukrainian Catholic Church in Canada, a gentleman whom I know very well, and he gives me the assurance that the matter is one that does require very serious and very immediate investigation. This in itself would be sufficient to convince me that the matter called for investigation. I rose, Mr. Chairman, simply to say that I am in hearty sympathy with the feelings of my friend the hon. member for Vegreville, and I thank him for having brought the matter to the attention of the committee and thus given us an opportunity of expressing our views with regard to it.

I also should like to join with hon. members on all sides of the house in congratulating the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luehkovich) on the very able presentation he has made to the house this afternoon of the case of the Ukrainian minority in Poland. I am quite sure that every member of the house will realize that the Ukrainian people of Canada and their compatriots in Poland have had a very able advocate to present their case here to-day. I have in my constituency probably ;hree or four hundred families of Ukrainians, and I have learned to admire them during my twenty years of close acquaintance with them.

I have found them hard-working, law-abiding, and very loyal. I was much relieved to hear from the lips of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that their troubles are receiving, or will shortly receive, the consideration of the council of the League of Nations, and I am sure we all hope that there will soon be a very happy ending 'to all their sufferings.

I do not know
that I can add anything useful to this debate except to say this: I believe that every member of the house, every Canadian who is a believer in minority rights-and every true Canadian is a true believer in minority rights -is concerned for the peace of the world and the happiness of mankind. In rising to congratulate the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luehkovich) for bringing this question to the attention of the house, perhaps I can best do so by saying that he made such a splendid advocacy of his case to-day that he proves himself to be the best example of the virtue and the capacity of the many Ukrainians who are citizens of Canada.
There are many of these people in my constituency, almost seven thousand. Ju^t before I left the west to come to attend to my duties here I was called upon by a number of influential Ukrainian residents in my constituency, who pointed out to me the extremity of their compatriots in Poland. May I say this, without any intention whatsoever of taking any side on the question, or of giving the slightest offence to any citizen, that when considering this important matter we do well to remember that it was a single shot fired in the capital of Serbia many years ago which precipitated the nations of the world into the Great war. Possibly there is a situation existing in Poland at the present time which, if it were not taken in hand by the League of Nations, might again precipitate the world into a wholesale war.
I am very glad indeed to learn from the lips of the right hon. the Prime Minister that he believes that the best thing which this country can do in the matter is to press it upon the attention of the League of Nations. The League of Nations is the proper tribunal, in fact the only tribunal we have, to work out this great problem of world peace. I am sure that the Prime Minister's announcement will be heard also with satisfaction by the hon. member for Vegreville, who asked in a very reasonable way simply that there might be an impartial tribunal before which this very serious question might be adjudicated upon and determined.

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. McIntosh
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	Before this question is finally
dealt with I would like to add a few words to what hon. members on both sides of the house have contributed to the debate.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) bring up this question concerning the condition of Ukrainians in Poland. The condition in that country at the present time is described as the sorest on the continent of Europe. Before I left for Ottawa from western Canada, while visiting some of the portions of my riding where Ukrainians have contributed a splendid part to the opening up of that part of Canada, I learned that it was the intention of the Ukrainian organization of western Canada to have the hon. member for Vegreville bring this question before parliament. At that time I said that no better man could bring such a subject to the attention of hon. members of this house. After his address this afternoon that is still my opinion. He made a splendid contribution to the debate, and I am sure his words will be read with interest from ocean to ocean.
While the hon. member was speaking, I thought his words brought two viewpoints before hon. members of this house. The hon. member himself belongs to an organization of his own people which links his people in western Canada to the homeland. The family connection between one's adopted land and one's motherland is always important. Any minority which will allow that bond to weaken will soon be submerged, and such a weakening might not be for the good of the nation of which they form a part. I believe that a nationality to be useful or to do a great work in any land must remember its motherland and also must be true to its adopted home. I believe the Ukrainians in western Canada are trying to follow that sound course. Then I thought of another connection between Canada and Poland, where we are told there is great trouble. I refer to the parliamentary connection, the discussions taking place in parliament, the activity of the League of Nations and the work of the committee which has been appointed by that league to make an investigation. When this discussion is over and the resolution is accepted, I hope the action of parliament will serve to strengthen the hands of those whom we shall send from Canada to attend the meeting of the League of Nations.

I was stating that I hope the discussion in parliament will be as emphatic as possible and that the action taken by parliament will 'be of a definite nature so that our representation in the League of Nations will be in a position diplomatically and emphatically to present to that organization the viewpoints of the Canadian people. If that is done I believe the investigation will be as full and complete as possible. In the event of the future continuation of the investigation which is now being carried on the record of the action of this parliament to-day will be of importance.
At this time I wish to say a few words about the Ukrainian citizens who compose a part of the population of the North Battleford constituency. These people constitute quite a colony in that federal area. They came into the district about twenty-five years ago and I consider it my privilege to-night to tell the house of the worthy contribution these people have made to the progress of that part of Saskatchewan. The district into which they came was considered anything but favourable. It was very undulating, quite rough, and was not supposed to be first class wheat land. However they came in to that section of northwestern Saskatchewan without money but with determination, fine vision and the high qualities of pioneers. They have done well. They have opened up that area and to-day it is a very productive wheat growing district, with splendid mixed farming possibilities. It can boast of many beautiful homes.
They have a fine patriotism; they have a great love for Canada; they are loyal citizens to king, country and to empire; they are industrious; they are law abiding and they are anxious to get along in life. They are people of integrity and honour; they are not materialistic but have high ideals and do not seem to have any great difficulty in adjusting themselves to their Canadian environment. They are men and women of vision, and that vision has arisen out of their adjustment to new conditions in this Dominion. They are not foreigners, as some people have called them, but they are as good Canadians as we have in Canada.
In that particular area of Saskatchewan the inception of the movement for better organization of those settlers took place many years

1422	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. McIntosh
ago and the effect of that organization, educationally and socially, has been wonderful. To-day most of the schools in these districts are manned by Ukrainian teachers who are doing good work among the rising generation, a generation which will be worthy of its new Canadian home. One ambition on the part of every father and mother is to send one or two of the family to the higher institutions of learning, to the universities and colleges. Today the children of Ukrainian families are competing favourably with the children of any other class of people in western Canada. At the present time they are doing great work and we look forward to greater work being done in the future. Last night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) made the statement that around the Maple Creek district there are areas of land which never should have been settled. And land broken up in a night would be breaking through a soil texture which could not be rebuilt perhaps in many years. I want to tell the minister that wherever Ukrainians have gone, whether the land has been rough or otherwise, they have broken through all difficulties. Whether it be to put fibre in the land, to build homes, to build educational institutions,1 to be thrifty and save money, to get ahead in life, to take part socially, educationally or otherwise in the building up of their country, the Ukrainians are on the job all the time and they can be thoroughly depended upon to do their work successfully.
I do not intend to go into the history of the Ukraine. The hon. member for Vegreville told us this afternoon that the Ukrainian people had a glorious past, that in days gone by they had a great and mighty kingdom, but that kingdom was overthrown, and from that time until the conclusion of the war in 1918 the Ukrainian people had never ceased their efforts to regain their lost sovereignty. But their hope that the treaty of Versailles would recognize their claims to self-determination were disappointed, and their country was included in the new Polish state, with the disastrous consequences to the Ukrainians that we have heard detailed this afternoon.
I believe it is the desire of all our Polish settlers in western Canada that the charges be investigated fully and that the good name of Poland be vindicated. On the other hand, our Ukrainian settlers feel that to a large extent their indictment can be substantiated, and they too want a thorough investigation, so that if they prove their case the League of Nations will take action and see that justice is done. But, Mr. Chairman, even if the present situation is adjusted in a manner satisfactory to the Ukrainians, I do not think it

will satisfy their aspirations, for they look forward to the day when their claim to selfdetermination will be recognized and they will become an autonomous nation.

Mr. Chairman, I hope
the hon. gentleman will pardon me, but he is now advocating something that the League of Nations distinctly says should not be done. I speak simply as the representative for the mtoment of the League of Nations. To suggest the erection of an autonomous community within another is forbidden by the league, and I appeal to the hon. gentleman not to place this parliament in the position of being censured by the League of Nations by taking a position that is wholly at variance with the principles of the league and its statutes with respect to this question to which we have acceded. It is not a matter of order, it is a matter of debate.
Mr. MeINTOSH: I was not attempting to link up parliament or the League of Nations with that viewpoint at all. I plainly stated that that was the viewpoint of the best educated Ukrainians in western Canada, but I am quite willing to deal with the question in a limited way, if, as the Prime Minister has intimated, if it will help forward a satisfactory settlement between the two peoples.
The minorities treaty is quite definite on what treatment, ought to be accorded to the Ukrainian people. Article 2 definitely states that, there must be protection of life and liberty; article 7 provides that all shall be equal before the law; it is also provided that the enjoyment of civil or political rights, as, for instance, the admission to public employments, functions and honours, or the exercise of professions and industries, must be guaranteed; and article 8 provides that the Polish nationals who belong to racial, religious or linguistic minorities shall enjoy the same treatment in law as the other Polish nationals, and particularly that they shall have an equal right to establish, manage and control at their own expense, charitable, religious and social institutions, schools, and other educational establishments, with liberty to use their own language and to exercise their own religion freely therein.
May I conclude, Mr. .Chairman, by expressing the hope that, when this question is brought before the League of Nations by the delegates from Canada, the report soon to be tabled by the committee of investigation appointed by the league will prove of such a nature that the aspirations of the Ukrainians will be realized, that harmony will grow out

of discord, and that not only will the Ukrain-f ian people feel satisfied, but that the adjustments between themselves and their Polish fellow citizens will be of such a nature as still further to promote the peace of the world.

Mr. Chairman, in
view of the many questions asked me by hon. gentlemen in the recess since six o'clock, I think it would be a good plan on my part to give some information to them, but before I do so I wish again to express my appreciation of all the speeches that have been delivered to-day on this question. Possibly in my presentation of the case I have been somewhat harsh, but that must be excused on the ground of the occasion and circumstance. When I came to Canada I was a boy of fifteen and I came alone. I hardly knew a single person in this country. And before I was fifteen I hardly knew that there were such people as Ukrainians in the world. I could not speak a word of Ukrainian.
I was asked to present the case on behalf of the Ukrainians in Canada, and the reason for that, I suppose, is that I am of the same descent. Many hon. members have discussed the subject to-day in a cultured and admirable manner and I should not like the opportunity to pass without congratulating them on the way they have presented it from their point of view. The hon. member for East Edmonton contributed a fine speech to the debate. I realize, Mr. Chairman, that the members of this house could not treat this question in any other than a spirit of fair play, for it would be folly for any hon. gentleman to make any appeal to race prejudice such as would aggravate or strain the relations between Poles and Ukrainians in Canada.
There is one matter to which I wish to refer, suggested by the remarks of the hon. member for East Edmonton. The hon. gentleman mentioned a letter received from the bishop of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic church.

Not the Greek Catholic
church, the Roman Catholic. ,

At any rate the
letter came from a bishop recommending a discussion of this matter in the House of Commons. May I state here that the former bishop of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic church, Bishop Budka, is now in eastern Galicia, and in a report which appeared in the Chicago Tribune of April 24 I find the following :
Bishop Nicetas Budka, fifteen years head of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic church of Canada, who was transferred back to Galicia, told me how, hearing of the "pacification

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Luchkovich
measures," he immediately went to the village where his invalid mother had been bedridden for two years. He found her sleeping on the floor in the remnants of her bed clothing. She had been tossed from bed by the soldiers, who ripped it to pieces searching for arms.
From this, hon. members will gather that even the former bishop of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic church in Canada has not been immune. If hon. members wish further information with respect to the technicalities and machinery provided by the League of Nations in regard to minorities, I suggest that they ask that very learned Canadian, Dr. Skelton; I am sure he would furnish it.
I would refer now for a moment or two to the manner in which petitions are presented and heard in the House of Commons. I was very much pleased to hear two great Canadian lawyers speak to-day on this subject, the right hon. the leader of the government and the former Minister of Justice. I do not know whether the right hon. the leader of the opposition is a lawyer, but I am under the impression that I have heard him on one or two occasions deprecate the fact that he was.

I am very
sorry I am not.

I was glad to hear
the matter presented so ably from the legal standpoint to-day. Now I wish to read from a report of the 36th convention of the International Law Association, and I am going to read this because there is a good deal of suspicion on the part of minorities about the way the League of Nations treat minority questions. These minorities believe that the success of the league in dealing with such questions is rather on a par with the performances of the surgeon who carries out a successful operation, althought it is reported that the patient died. I shall read this report as I have it:
Thirty-Sixth Convention Of International Law
Association
Held at the house of the Association of the Bar at 42 West 44th street, New York City, September 2 to September 10, 1930.
Session of September 8,	1930, subject
"Minorities" (as reported in New York Times September 9, 1930.)
Jurists Ask Leave To Help Minorities
World Law Session Proposes Permanent Commission to Protect Racial Groups Finds War Peril In Unrest
Geneva's Handling of Dominated Peoples' Protests is Criticized
With a warning before them that the plight of minorities in central Europe was dangerous to world peace, the jurists of the International Law Association, representing a score of countries, called upon the League of Nations yesterday to create a permanent minorities' commission to protect subordinate racial groups and investigate discriminations against them.

Coupled with the association's request was a criticism of present procedure before the league in relation to the disposition of protests from minorities. Provision was not yet adequate for proper publicity on the findings in each case, the jurists held, and protestants had no opportunity to reply to an official defence presented by the government in question.
The -warning of impending peril in the makeup of the European map was enunciated by Dr. Paul de Auer, leader of the Hungarian Peace Society and counsel to the Bank of France. Despite the American slogan, "selfdetermination of nations," in the world war, the peace treaties had left a larger number of peoples living under foreign domination than before the war, he declared.
Sees World Peace in Danger
"Self-determination has not been respected," he continued. "Millions and millions of population have been simply transferred into other countries, incorporated in other states, without having been asked, without having been given the opportunity of self-determination by plebiscite.
"The atmosphere will not be clear in central and eastern. Europe until minority questions are satisfactorily settled. The present discontent of great masses leads to permanent uneasiness and is dangerous not only to the minorities but chiefly to the States to which they belong and to the peace of Europe and the world."
The request directed to the League of Nations was embodied in a report of a committee headed by R. E. L. Vaughan Williams of England which was adopted unanimously. A permanent minorities' commission of the league, the report says, could insist upon the preservation to minorities of such fundamental rights of justice and equality before the law as are set forth in the minorities' protection treaties.
_ The report also suggests that the commission should have power to investigate as to whether there are infringements of the guaranteed protections.
"It has been alleged," says the report, "that certain laws indirectly and in a disguised form affect minorities unfairly; that by certain laws a discretion is given to the administrative authorities who act in an arbitrary manner unfair to minorities; that there are no proper provisions for appealing by due process of law against administrative decisions; that minorities are not given their fair share of land under agrarian reform; that educational facili ties are denied to minorities in respect to their language; that the free exercise of their religion has been denied to certain communities in breach of the treaty rights.
"Your committee, while of course expressing no opinion, as to the facts alleged, feel strongly that it is for the good of the states concerned, no less than for that of the minorities, and in the best interests of peace, that such charges should be investigated in the manner above suggested."
To .buttress what has been said in this report I will quote an article which is very-pertinent to the question, as it appeared in the Manchester Guardian some time ago:
Amongst the Ukrainian petitions submitted to the league there was one drafted and signed by Mme. Milena Rudnicka, who is well known

Ukrainians in Poland-
-Mr. Luchkovich
in the international women's movement as a person of high intelligence, integrity and heroism. Amongst very many petitions sent in to the league since the "pacification" (as the Polish excesses committed in the Ukraine last October are officially termed) here is one of the few that have been carefully and intelligently drafted. It also included the most comprehensive record that has yet been made of the "pacification." 1 have referred to this report in a previous message-it is a document of about eighty pages of typescript, and is oi fundamental importance (it was included in the interpellation made by the Ukrainian members of the Polish parliament). Indeed, to disregard this document would be a grave if not a fatal omission in any inquiry into the subject.
I now learn that the league secretariat has formally declined to regard Mme. Rudnieka's petition as "receivable." So far six Ukrainian petitions have been declared "receivable." One of these six is a flimsy document by a Ukrainian resident in Paris. There is good reason to believe that some, at least, of the others are also badly drafted, and feebly provided with documentary evidence.
It is possible that the report embodied in Mme. Rudnicka's petition is embodied in one or more of the other petitions also, in which case it is too early to say that this report will not be dealt with by the league. But the fate of Mme. Rudnicka's petition is bound to raise grave doubts as to the way petitions are treated by the secretariat. The number of Ukrainian petitions sent in within the last few months grows into hundreds; to pick out a few of inferior quality that can easily be pulled to pieces by those astute people who are anxious that nothing may come of any Ukrainian petition would not be particularly high-minded. To say that this has actually happened would be premature.
Why Mme. Rudnicka's petition has been rejected is not stated. It certainly conforms to at least four out of the five conditions that were laid down by a resolution of the league council in September, 1923

 (1) that its purpose is the protection of the minorities in conformity with the treaties; (2) that it is not put in the form of a demand for a rupture of political ties between the minority in question and the state of which that minority is a part; (3) that it does not emanate from an anonymous or doubtful source; (4) that it contains matter which has not been the subject of previous petitions; (5) that it is drawn up without violence of language.
None of these five points has been left unfulfilled in Mme. Rudnicka's petition with the possible exception of the fourth. If a previous petition that had been declared "receivable" includes the eighty-page report then little harm will have been done. But if not, then Mme. Rudnicka's petition will have conformed to the fourth point also, for the report is new material. In that case the rejection of Mme. Rudnicka's petition would be a great wrong.
Additional facilities for the hearing of petitions by the League of Nations should be provided. There are four matters to which I would direct the attention of hon. members as pertinent and relevant to the case. They are as follows:
Woodrow Wilson's fourteen points.
Treaty of Versailles.
Decision of the Council of Ambassadors.
The Minority treaty.
Under the first heading I would refer to the following:
Number 10. The peoples of Austria-Hungary, whose place among the nations we wish to see safeguarded and assured, should be accorded the freest opportunity of autonomous development.
Number 13. An independent Polish state should be erected which should include the territories inhabited by indisputably Polish populations, which should be assured a free and secure access to the sea, and whose political and economic independence and territorial integrity should be guaranteed by international covenant.
(Promulgated in address to congress, January 8, 1918).
Under the second heading, Treaty of Versailles, I quote the following:
Article 93.	.
Poland accepts and agrees to embody in a treaty with the principal allied and associated powers such provisions as may be deemed necessary by the said powers to protect the interests of inhabitants of Poland who differ from the majority of population in race, language, or religion.
(Signed, June 28, 1919).
This treaty is often confused with the minorities' treaty, but they were separate treaties although signed on the same day. The third document to which I desire to make reference, the Decision of the Council of Ambassadors, reads in part as follows:
The British Empire, France, Italy and Japan, signatories, together with the United States, as principal allied and associated powers, to the treaty of Versailles:
Whereas, according to the terms of article 37, paragraph 3, of the above treaty they shall establish the frontiers of Poland, not specified in that treaty.
I am reading only those parts which refer to the subject matter under discussion. The document continues:
Whereas, Poland has recognized that as Eastern Galicia, the ethnographical conditions make a regime of autonomy necessary;
Autonomy has been promised to the Ukrainians in the western Ukraine and in eastern Galicia. The document continues:
Whereas, the treaty between the principal allied and associated powers and Poland, signed June 28, 1919, provides in all territories placed under Polish sovereignty special guarantees in favour of racial, linguistic, or religious minorities.
I will not read the remaining paragraphs as they do not relate to this matter. That document was signed by the Polish plenipotentiary, Maurice Zamoyski at Paris on March 15, 1923. I will not quote from the minorities, treaty because it has been referred to already, not only by myself but by other hon. members. I would also like to quote an article by Mr. H. Wickham Steed. This appeared in the Review of Reviews of December 15,
1426	COMMONS
Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Bennett
1930, and presents such a good case for the Ukrainians that I feel I must read it. It i3 as follows:
The Case of Poland. In no country is the precise and impartial ascertainment of facts more necessary than it is in Poland, and no country has a . greater interest in presenting to the world an irrefutable case. Polish methods of repressing incendiarism and other acts of sabotage, of which sundry Ukrainian groups were guilty last Autumn in east Galicia, have been brutal to a degree which reasonable Poles are the first to deplore and condemn. While it may be true that these acts were instigated or encouraged from Berlin, the fact that they were committed justifies neither the neglect of the Polish government to remove legitimate Ukrainian grievances, nor its folly in playing into the hands of its enemies by dragooning whole Ukrainian districts. The folly was the greater because it strengthened the hands of Poland's detractors who lose no opportunity of declaiming against the Polish corridor and the Upper Silesian settlement. The case of the Polish corridor is far stronger than the public in western Europe and in the United States understands. Poland has nothing to lose by an impartial ascertainment of the facts concerning it and, especially in regard to the position of east Prussia. But Poland or rather the "Cabinet of Colonels" by which Marshal Pilsudski has thought fit to surround himself, chills many sympathies by the adoption of methods similar to those employed by the old bolshevist regime in Russia or by the fascist dictatorship in Italy.
This is all I have to say on this subject at the present time. May I conclude by again extending my thanks to all hon. members who have participated in this debate. The people who asked me to sponsor this presentation appreciate the opportunity afforded, and I extend their thanks to the right hon. the Prime Minister and the right hon. the leader of the opposition for helping to facilitate the discussion on the minorities question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is perhaps desirable that I should make two or three additional observations, not to trespass upon the time of the committee but rather to clarify a situation which I think has been somewhat obscured by reason of the fact that there is an earnest desire on the part of a large number of hon. members in this house to indicate their sympathy with a people so largely represented in their constituencies.
We might as well realize that this country is a member of the League of Nations and that accredited to this country at the moment are several Polish consuls. As regards the Ukrainians, as the hon. member for Vegreville pointed out, they are at present, so far as we are concerned, citizens of Poland. That is one of the difficulties which the house has not frankly realized.

When you begin to discuss the internal government of a friendly power, you are on very dangerous ground. It is not the duty of this Dominion to undertake to advise people how they should govern themselves. That is their business. On the other hand, there is an obligation upon us as a member of the League of Nations, and it is a rather serious obligation, not to reflect upon the other members of that league, and hon. gentlemen have been fair enough to realize that. The league having now undertaken a responsibility-and a very serious one it is-must carry it through, and we may find ourselves at the appropriate moment voting to determine what action the league shall take. Therefore it is of the utmost importance that an open mind should be kept with regard to these problems.
I certainly sympathize with the hon. member for Vegreville. As he said, he might be pardoned for taking a strong view with respect to this matter. Would one not expect him to do so? Would one not expect any young man who came to this country at the age of fifteen of the same stock as the people of whom he speaks, to have a strong view with respect to the matter? We know that under similar circumstances we would, and we expect it in his. There is a great difference between Canada and other countries on this continent in this regard. Under our constitution, if the rights of minorities are affected, recourse may be had to the courts. Barrett vs. the City of Winnipeg is the outstanding case on the subject. In that case the privy council decided there had been a prejudicial interference with minority rights with respect to education in the province of Manitoba. Later the privy council decided that the minority was entitled, under the provisions of section 93 of the British North America Act, to remedial legislation. There you have a tribunal which determined that rights had been taken from the minority and, secondly, that the minority had a right of redress under the constitution itself. That is where the position is not analogous to that of the Ukrainians in Poland, for it is not the constitution of Poland that is concerned, but a treaty made by the country to which they owe allegiance with other countries of the world. Thus far no international court has been set up that can by adequate and appropriate sanctions take effective action in cases of violations of treaties. In other words, the science of international law has not reached the stage in its development where a court of international justice, by its judgment, is able to decree and carry into effect a decree with respect to the violation of treaty rights by the government, over a portion of the population it governs.

Ukrainians in Poland-Mr. Bennett
There is the clear distinction. It is unnecessary to remind the house that during the last few years great progress has been made. There has been a persistent and continuous endeavour on the part of representatives of all democracies to ensure that some tribunal be set up that might not only have the jurisdiction to determine matters of this kind but also have power by appropriate sanctions to see that its decrees were enforced. That time has not yet arrived in our developement in international affairs. Perhaps later, during the discussion of the General Act, I may have occasion, to make a few observations, but at the moment may I again assure the hon. gentleman that the delegation which represents Canada at the next meeting of the league will do everything that can be done to ensure that justice-and who would not like to see justice attained and who does not know hoiw difficult it is of attainment?-is done alike to the Ukrainians and the country of which they are citizens.
I could not, of course, in the position which I occupy for a single moment, permit without at least some protest, anything to be said that would indicate that, the parliament of Canada was seeking by any intervention on its part to secure the setting up of a new government by a portion of the population of Poland. To do that would be ruinous to the position of this Dominion as a member of the League of Nations. If I might say so, I know from what the hon. member for Vegre-ville has said to me, he thoroughly appreciates that position, thoroughly understands the implications of it, and he has very well refrained from making that suggestion, except as it might be inferentially understood from what was said by another and not by himself in one of the quotations read into the record. That being the case, I am sure a very useful purpose has been served by this discussion. I trust not the least useful part of it has been that part which has brought home to us a sense of our own responsibilities and also, so far as it may be possible, by a country new in international affairs, a realization of what age-old conflicts, conflicts that are not a century but sometimes several centuries old, mean. Those who followed the history of the great war, and remember the battle between the Serbs and the Turks, will recall that in the opening sentence of the history of that time, we are reminded that the success by the Serbs meant victory in the conflict that had been waged for centuries. So it is that we have here age-old animosities, age-old difficulties that will not be solved in a single minute, and least of all by a new
democracy 4,000 miles away from the spot where the differences arise. If the discussion has brought to our minds that sense of responsibility, it has certainly been useful.
It has also been useful inasmuch as it has brought to our attention the fact that there are two sides to every question. When the hon. member referred to the pamphlet that .had been issued on behalf of the Ukrainians and in the next breath referred to the pamphlet issued on behalf of the Poles and their counter-allegations, he made the case complete, and we are not judges in Israel or elsewhere. Least of all are we judges of the conditions in Poland, because if we accept one story, we must arrive at one conclusion, and if we accept the other, we must arrive at a different conclusion.
As I said a moment ago, humanly speaking there is nothing so difficult to attain as justice, for it is not easy for any of us to think in terms of absolute righteousness and justice. In this instance we are not abrogating to ourselves the right to determine where justice lies between two contending parties. We can only say that men, women and children numbering 300,000 or thereabouts in this Dominion are interested in the welfare of their kinspeople in the land whence they came, believe they are not receiving their rights under the treaty that Poland made with the nations of the world, and ask at our hands that every possible facility be provided to make known the extent to which that treaty has been violated, if at all, and what would be the appropriate steps to take if it is established that there has been a violation of its provisions. That, I think, has been the result of this discussion. So far as the government is concerned, it will endeavour to the best of its ability to see that those who represent Canada make known the claims that have been presented so admirably, if at times with some feeling, as the hon. gentleman said, a feeling which we can rightly and properly understand, to those who have the enormous, the tremendous responsibility of determining the rights of contending parties in order that justice, the end aimed at, may be done to all.

Just a parting word. When I broached this subject first to both the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition, I told them that it was with no intention of putting something over parliament. I have presented the facts .as I got them from certain parties. Whether they are true or not, it is not for me to say. I hope that the committee of three will find out whether the allegations are right or wrong.
Supply-External Affairs

If they are wrong, I shall be glad to know it; if they are right, I shall be glad to know it. I hope they are right, but if they are wrong, I shall be one of the first to admit that they are wrong. With respect to my relations to Canada and my relations to the country whence my parents sprang, I should like to tell this house that my first loyalty is to Canada and I say quite sincerely to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the members of this house, that if those relations should conflict the Ukraine would have to be forgotten because I am first of all a citizen of Canada and to her I owe my absolute loyalty.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: The amount of 8122,000 is required to provide for the government's share of the cost of completing the interprovincial bridge now being constructed over the Ottawa river at Hawkesbury. An order in council was passed on August 5 accepting the lowest regular tender of Farley and Grant.
Up to what date were the tenders received?
I have not that information.
What wages were supposed to be paid to the labourers on that work?
The schedules are from time to time procured from the Labour department, and are attached to and made a part of the contract.

There was a schedule
attached to this contract when it was awarded. I hold in my hand one of those schedules, and according to the schedule the wages to be paid to the labourers on that work were 45 cents an hour. Later, the contractor who was awarded the contract paid the labourers only 35 cents an hour. Complaints were made by the labourers from Hawkesbury, and after considerable correspondence had been exchanged between the Department of Labour, the Department of Public Works, and the interested labourers, an additional five cents was remitted to these men; which proves that a reasonable wage was not being paid to the labourers. Now they have applied to the Minister of Labour for the 45 cents an hour which they were originally supposed to get.
I am under the impression that this schedule which I have here, lowing a rate of 45 cents an hour, was even placarded on the works.
I shall not take time to read all this correspondence which I have here. I will simply say that the Minister of Labour wrote that he was fixing a rate of 40 cents an hour. This trouble over the wage rate has created a lot of uneasiness in the district. The contractors knew very well when they submitted their tender that they were expected to pay 45 cents an hour for labourers. Later on, as I said, the Minister of Labour decided that 40 cents an hour was a reasonable wage on this work. As the Minister of Labour has not a seat in this house I appeal to the Minister of Public Works. The contractor most certainly based his price, when submitting his tender, upon a labour cost of 45 cents an hour. The labourers received only 35 cents an hour, and later five cents an hour more was added.

Supply-Public Works-Bridges
There is an additional five cents an hour not accounted for. The labourer has not got it, and the labourers are asking themselves if the government is taking the part of the contractor rather than supporting the interests of the labourers. If that is not the case, where did this other five cents go to?

My understanding is that the rates are determined by the prevailing rate of wages in the locality where the work is done. This is an interprovincial bridge, and possibly there is some difference between the rate in the Province of Ontario and the rate in the province of Quebec. Such differences are adjusted through the Department of Labour. I can assure my hon. friend that the Public Works department sees to it, wherever complaints are made, that the provisions of the contract in respect to the payment of labour are carried out. The Minister of Labour is really the referee in the matter. He is the one to whom we refer and with whom we consult when conditions of this kind arise. I shall draw this matter to his attention and have it further investigated.

Before the tenders were called for, the Department of Labour sent a representative to Hawkesbury, and I believe he made an investigation and a report to the Department of Public Works. The report states the different salaries to be paid to the different trades or classes of labour employed. In the report attached to the tenders it is stated very plainly that labourers are to be paid 45 cents per hour.

I do not know
whether they have been or not. If there is a complaint I suggest it be made to the Department of Labour; that department will take up the matter with the Department of Public Works and if possible have it adjusted.
I would not like to retard the progress of the item, but would the minister allow me to produce correspondence to show that they were not paid 45 cents?

I should be glad if my hon. friend would furnish me with evidence that the contractor had not fulfilled his contract with respect to the payment of labour. We are in a position to investigate the matter, ascertain through the Department of Labour what has been done, and adjust grievances where it is possible to do so.

I think the minister ought to be satisfied that the price stated in the schedule to be paid to this class of
labour was 45 cents per hour. May I read a letter written by the contractor on February 20, 193.1 to one of the interested parties: Re: Hawkesbury-Grenville Bridge
The matter of wage rates for labourers on the above work has been determined by the Department of Labour to be forty cents (0.40c.) per hour.
It was fixed at 45 cents, and as I said a minute ago it was revised by the Department of Labour some time in February and placed at 40 cents.
You worked in 1930 a total of 5104 houra for which you were paid at the rate of 0.35 cents per hour. There is therefore coming to you an amount of 5104 hours at 0.05 cents per hour or a total of $25.52 for which you will find our cheque No. 5227 dated April 15, 1931.
Then there is a section of the letter which I shall not read. It is more or less of a personal character. Then, to continue:
Enclosed you will find duplicate receipt forms which we would ask you to sign and return to this office immediately upon receipt of enclosed cheque dated April 15, 1931.
The situation is that when the 5 cents was refunded each and every man was compelled to sign a receipt in duplicate so that he would not have any come-back on the contractors for the original rate. Before the signing of the receipt this contractor was sure that the Department of Labour would refix the salary at 40 cents per hour, instead of adhering to the first schedule on which they had based their price when they bid at the rate of 45 cents per hour. If these contractors bid having in mind the fact that they were to pay the labourers 45 cents per hour and if the labourers did not get the last 5 cents, where did that 5 cents go? I would ask the Department of Public Works if in that instance they are not especially protecting the contractors.

The rates for
labour are not based upon the estimates of what contractors propose to pay. They are based upon what the Department of Labour considers a fair and reasonable wage, and if the contractor makes his estimates too low, he is the loser.

I am not quite satisfied with the answer made by the minister. Supposing the schedule had been fixed at $1 per hour for labourers, would the minister suggest that the contractor would have fixed the same unit price to do that work?

Again I would say to my hon. friend that we are not controlled by the action of the contractors. We are controlled by what is considered a reasonable, fair and decent wage in the locality,

and that figure we secure for labourers regardless of what the estimate of the contractors may be. I am sure if the contractor estimated his wages so much above the current rate he would not be the lowest tenderer. We have no way of learning what the contractor's estimate was, and we decline to be bound by it.

Does the minister say that in spite of the schedule providing for 45 cents per hour these labourers will have to be satisfied with 40 cents per hour because they were paid 35 cents in the first place and the Department of Labour requested a payment of 5 cents more? When the cheques were handed over for the payment of the last 5 cents these men were compelled to sign a duplicate receipt in order to show that they would have no further claim.
I can only repeat that the Department of Labour is organized for the protection of labour.
It is not protecting in this case.

In this case
whatever rate the Department of Labour has determined is reasonable and proper under the circumstances must be the schedule prevailing. On that basis payment must be made.

I thank the minister

cents in full discharge of all claims, so that later they would not be able to claim the original rate.

Is it not a fact that when
a proposed work is to be undertaken the chief engineer of the Department of Public Works invites the resident district or provincial engineer, as the case may be, to state the local scale of wages? Then if the scale is higher than that on which the cost is estimated, the estimates are revised before tenders are called for, so that anybody wishing to tender can ascertain from the district engineer what the wages will be and tender accordingly. If in this case they tendered on a wage scale of 45 cents, and are now allowed by the Department of Labour to pay 40 cents, they are making that much more profit out of the labouring men than they intended to do. I hold in my hand a specimen of the form sent out to the district engineer, and it contains this paragraph:

Then the scale is set forth for carpenters, blacksmiths, driver with horse and cart, driver with team and wagon, and so on, and there is a request to be advised if these rates will affect the estimates cost. If the minister is satisfied bo let the item stand so that he may investigate the matter, I will not deal with other objections for the moment.

I cannot do
more than again assure my hon. friend that that matter will be taken up by the Labour department in the light of the terms of the contract, and justice will be done these men. My hon. friend suggests that we may be taking the part of the contractors. I assure him that nothing of that kind is being done; we feel that our first duty is to protect labour.
Carried.

The more my hon.
friends opposite say "carried" probably the further I will go. I think I have been fair to the minister. I have not given a single name, I have not tried to put anybody in the hole. All I have asked is that these labourers at Hawkesbury be treated fairly. If hon. gentlemen opposite are not satisfied with this method, I can do it otherwise.
Go to it.

Dear Sir,

I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of February 23, as regards the scale of wages in connection with the contract for the Hawkes-bury-Grenville bridge, I noted carefully the various points to which my attention was drawn. This letter is written in French and signed by Mr. Ward, Deputy Minister of Labour. He states very plainly that a decision was given, that he reconsidered it again, and refers to a previous letter of February 13th.
Mr. D'UFF: Read the letter.

It is as follows:
Ottawa, February 13, 1931
Mr. Romeo Bazinet,
"The Bridge Workers,"
P.O. Box 73,
Hawkesbury, Ont.
Dear Sir,-
I am directed by the Minister of Labour to acknowledge receipt of your letter dated on the 9th instant, enclosing copy of the proceedings of the meeting held by workers employed oh the construction of the Hawkesbury-Gren-ville bridge, as well as a list of the employees present at that meeting, and recommending to the department the wage rates which have been referred to.
It w'ould perhaps be of interest to you and the workers whom you represent, to know that not one single claim was received from the workers employed on the contract of the Hawlcesbury-Grenville bridge, while the work was being carried out, and that, in fact, no complaint reached us before many weeks had passed after the work had been discontinued, for the season at least. Long before claims were received the department on its own initiative ....
I wish to draw your attention to this passage for although it was stated that there had been no complaints, there had really been complaints made, as this part of the letter will show:
Long before claims were received, the department on its own initiative carried out inquiries, among others, one in connection with the contract aforesaid, following which it prepared a statement including the name of each worker employed, the total working hours, the rate per hour and total payments received.

The lower rates mentioned paid, as it appears from the information gathered by us, refer evidently to unskilled labour.
In this connection, I should mention that as a whole the remuneration of unskilled labour in the province of Quebec is inferior to that paid Ontario. In the present case the contract refers to the construction of the substructure of the bridge linking the two provinces, the labour engaged in this work having been distributed as evenly as possible between the two provinces.
Moreover, we believe that there existed no drawn line as to work to be done by each of these two groups of workmen, and the work was equally interchangeable.
Under these circumstances and others, it is believed that 40 cents per hour is considered a fair and reasonable rate for unskilled labour and is higher, we think, than that paid at present either at Hawkesbury or across the river. We shall therefore see that each worker receives, in due time, a cheque covering the increase of the additional amount of 5 cents per hour for the period of work done by each one, that is the difference between the old rate of 35 cents and the fixed rate of 40 cents per hour.
With reference to information required as to the responsibilities of sub-contractors and rates for overtime, when the regular day's work is over, I must inform you that the rates fixed by contract apply exclusively to the work on the substructure.
A clause in the contract with reference to work fixes a maximum of 8 hours per day, however, no penalties are provided as to overtime work. May I, in this connection, point out that never during the execution of the work was the department apprised that the 8 hour day was not observed, otherwise we would have immediately taken steps to have the provisions of the contract, as regards working hours, strictly carried out.
Yours truly,
H. H. Ward,
Deputy Minister of Labour.
The deputy minister in this letter has fixed the wages, at 40 cents an hour whereas previously it was 45 cents; so that there is a difference of five cents. But as the hon. member for Gloucester stated a few minutes ago, when these tenders were put in the price was fixed in accordance with the wages which they were supposed to pay to the labourers. This schedule was attached to their contract. In the county of Prescott the contractors paid only 35 cents an hour, and of course the men complained. Now we find that the Department of Labour on February 13 fixed their wages at 40 cents. The reason the people are so greatly dissatisfied is that the contractors are able to make a profit of 5 cents an hour on all the hours of labour put in by the men. That 5 cents the labourers lose, and besides they are asked to sign receipts to say that they have no further claim.
These labourers have not been treated fairly and they are complaining. I tell the minister quite frankly that they are very uneasy about

it. They claim that the government is helping the big interests as against the interest of the labourers. I did not, wish to mention this, and if the minister had allowed the item to stand, on the understanding that further information would be provided, I would not have done so. I have not a copy of the receipt which they were asked to sign, but the receipts were made out in duplicate and were returned to the contractors at the time the cheques were issued. Some hon. member has asked whether I have a copy of the receipt which the men had to sign. I have not, but in the letter from the contractors to the labourers this statement appears:
Enclosed you will find duplicate receipt forms which we would ask you to sign and return to this office immediately.
Once again I urge upon the minister the importance of looking into this matter with a view to finding, if possible, some means of doing justice to the men employed on the construction of that bridge. I am speaking for the men from the province of Ontario; I am not speaking for the Quebec side. It is now practically eleven o'clock and I should be glad if the minister would undertake to furnish the information I have asked for.

I assure my hon. friend, as I have assured every hon. member, that I am prepared to give all the information available, and I cannot understand the suggestion that I am seeking to withhold anything. This is the first I have heard of this complaint and I have promised the hon. gentleman to take the matter up with the Department of Labour and try to get the facts and give them to him. I have no objection to the item standing, and have never endeavoured to press it through. I move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
